written.text: What is alternation of generation?
modelAnswer: Alternation of generations is a life cycle in which the haploid gametophyte and diploid sporophyte generations alternate.
The gametophyte produces gametes, while the sporophyte produces spores.
written.followUp: Differentiate between a haploid and a diploid generation.

rubric.why: Awards one mark for identifying the two generations that alternate.
rubric.description: The life cycle alternates between gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
rubric.how: Look for both generation names and their alternation.

rubric.why: Awards one mark for stating their ploidy difference.
rubric.description: The gametophyte is haploid and the sporophyte is diploid.
rubric.how: Look for the correct haploid/diploid distinction.

written.text: Differentiate between anabolism and catabolism.
modelAnswer: Anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler molecules and usually requires energy.
Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler molecules and usually releases energy.
written.followUp: Differentiate between photosynthesis and respiration in terms of energy change.

rubric.why: Anabolism forms complex molecules from simpler ones.
rubric.description: Describes anabolism as building complex molecules from simpler molecules.
rubric.how: Award for stating that anabolism builds or synthesises complex molecules from simpler molecules.

rubric.why: Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones.
rubric.description: Describes catabolism as breaking complex molecules into simpler molecules.
rubric.how: Award for stating that catabolism breaks down or degrades complex molecules into simpler molecules.

written.text: Define activation energy.
modelAnswer: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy required to start a chemical reaction.
written.followUp: What is the role of enzymes in lowering the energy needed for a reaction?

rubric.why: Identifies activation energy as the minimum energy required.
rubric.description: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy required.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the minimum energy.

rubric.why: Links the required energy to starting a reaction.
rubric.description: This energy is required to start a chemical reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the energy is needed to start a chemical reaction.

written.text: Differentiate between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration occurs in the presence of oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water.
Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen; it produces lactic acid in muscles, or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast.
written.followUp: Give one difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration and state one product of each.

rubric.why: Aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen, while anaerobic respiration takes place without oxygen.
rubric.description: Distinguishes the processes by their oxygen requirement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the oxygen requirement of both processes.

rubric.why: Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid in muscles or ethanol in yeast.
rubric.description: States the products of aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the aerobic products and at least one correct anaerobic product.

written.text: Define Bioenergetics.
modelAnswer: Bioenergetics is the study of energy transformations in living organisms.
written.followUp: What is meant by energy transformation in living organisms?

rubric.why: Bioenergetics concerns energy and its transformations.
rubric.description: Identifies energy as the subject of bioenergetics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to the study of energy or energy transformations.

rubric.why: Bioenergetics studies these processes in living organisms.
rubric.description: Specifies the biological context.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the study concerns living organisms.

written.text: Define photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use sunlight and chlorophyll to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
Oxygen is released during the process.
written.followUp: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: These are the essential raw materials and product of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Names carbon dioxide and water as materials used to make glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the reactants and glucose product.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis uses light energy captured by chlorophyll.
rubric.description: States that the process uses sunlight and chlorophyll.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning sunlight and chlorophyll.

written.text: Differentiate between source and sink.
modelAnswer: A source is a plant part, such as a leaf, that produces or releases sugars for transport.
A sink is a plant part, such as a root or fruit, that uses or stores transported sugars.
written.followUp: Differentiate between xylem and phloem.

rubric.why: Defines a source by its role in supplying sugars.
rubric.description: A source is a plant part that produces or releases sugars for transport, such as a leaf.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that a source supplies sugars.

rubric.why: Defines a sink by its role in using or storing sugars.
rubric.description: A sink is a plant part that uses or stores transported sugars, such as a root or fruit.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that a sink uses or stores sugars.

written.text: Define nutrition.
modelAnswer: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain food and use it for energy, growth, repair and maintenance of the body.
written.followUp: Define heterotrophic nutrition.

rubric.why: Identifies nutrition as the process of obtaining and using food.
rubric.description: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining nutrition as obtaining and using food.

rubric.why: Gives a valid purpose for using food.
rubric.description: Food is used for energy, growth, repair or maintenance of the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating at least one valid purpose of food.

written.text: Define Transpirational Pull.
modelAnswer: Transpirational pull is the force produced by water loss from leaves during transpiration.
It draws water upward from the roots through the xylem.
written.followUp: Define transpiration and state one factor that affects its rate.

rubric.why: Shows that transpiration from leaves creates the pull.
rubric.description: Cause of the pull
rubric.how: Award for linking the pull to water loss or evaporation from the leaves.

rubric.why: Identifies the upward movement of water through the plant.
rubric.description: Definition
rubric.how: Award for describing the force that draws water upward through xylem, from roots toward leaves.

written.text:
(a) Define binomial nomenclature. Describe its significance.
(b) Write the types and Functions of Endoplasmic Reticulum.
modelAnswer: (a) Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two word scientific name: the first word is its genus and the second its species.
It provides a standard name that is used internationally.
It avoids confusion caused by different common or local names.
The two-part name identifies an organism and shows the genus to which it belongs.
(b) The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membranous channels in the cytoplasm. It is of two types:
Rough ER has ribosomes on its surface and helps in protein synthesis and transport.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes and helps in lipid synthesis; it also has roles in detoxification and calcium storage.
written.followUp: State the rules for writing genus and species names in binomial nomenclature.

rubric.why: The definition must state that the scientific name has two parts, genus and species.
rubric.description: (a) Defines binomial nomenclature as a two-word scientific name made up of genus and species.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the two-part scientific name and its genus and species components.

rubric.why: Scientific names provide a standard name used internationally.
rubric.description: (a) States that the naming system is standard and internationally accepted.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its universal use.

rubric.why: A standard name prevents confusion caused by differing common or local names.
rubric.description: (a) Explains that binomial nomenclature avoids confusion from common or local names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this significance.

rubric.why: The name identifies an organism and shows the genus to which it belongs.
rubric.description: (a) States that the name identifies the organism or indicates its genus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its identification or classification value.

rubric.why: Identifies rough ER by its ribosomes.
rubric.description: (b) Names rough endoplasmic reticulum and notes that ribosomes are attached to it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and its distinguishing feature.

rubric.why: Rough ER is associated with protein synthesis and movement of proteins.
rubric.description: (b) States a valid function of rough ER, such as protein synthesis or transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct rough-ER function.

rubric.why: Identifies smooth ER by the absence of ribosomes.
rubric.description: (b) Names smooth endoplasmic reticulum and notes that ribosomes are absent from its surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and its distinguishing feature.

rubric.why: Smooth ER performs functions distinct from rough ER.
rubric.description: (b) States a valid function of smooth ER, such as lipid synthesis, detoxification or calcium storage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct smooth-ER function.

written.text:
(a) Proteins and Lipids are the best source of energy. Interpret.
(b) Define Enzyme. Write the temperature as a factor affecting the rate of Enzyme Action.
modelAnswer: (a) When food molecules are oxidized in cells, their chemical energy is released.
One gram of lipid yields about 9 kcal, while one gram of protein yields about 4 kcal.
One gram of carbohydrate also yields about 4 kcal.
Therefore, lipids are the most concentrated energy source per gram; the statement is not fully correct if it calls proteins the best energy source as well.
Proteins can be used for energy, but their main roles are growth and repair, and they are not normally the body's preferred fuel.
(b) An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions in living organisms.
As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more frequently, so the reaction rate increases.
The rate reaches its maximum at the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature and its active site changes shape, causing the rate to decrease.
written.followUp: Compare the energy released by the oxidation of one gram of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.

rubric.why: Gives the energy yield of lipids and identifies their high energy value.
rubric.description: (a) Lipids yield about 9 kcal per gram, the greatest energy yield among these food groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the value and 1 mark for identifying lipids as the highest-yielding.

rubric.why: Gives the energy yield of proteins.
rubric.description: (a) Proteins yield about 4 kcal per gram.
rubric.how: Award for the correct approximate value.

rubric.why: Provides the comparison needed to interpret the claim.
rubric.description: (a) Carbohydrates also yield about 4 kcal per gram.
rubric.how: Award for the correct approximate value.

rubric.why: Clarifies the role of proteins rather than treating them as the body's preferred fuel.
rubric.description: (a) Proteins are mainly used for growth and repair; they can provide energy, but are not normally the preferred energy source.
rubric.how: Award for stating the main structural role or that proteins are not the preferred fuel.

rubric.why: Defines an enzyme by its role as a catalyst in living organisms.
rubric.description: (b) An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining an enzyme as a biological catalyst.

rubric.why: Explains why enzyme action initially increases with temperature.
rubric.description: (b) As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more frequently, increasing the reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased kinetic energy to more frequent collisions.

rubric.why: Identifies the temperature at which enzyme activity reaches its maximum.
rubric.description: (b) The rate reaches its maximum at the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the optimum temperature or maximum activity.

rubric.why: Explains the decrease in enzyme activity above the optimum temperature.
rubric.description: (b) Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature, changing its active site and decreasing the reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting denaturation or a changed active site with a decrease in rate.

written.text:
(a) How would you relate the internal structure of root with the uptake of water and salts?
(b) Describe the ways by which humans can grow new plants by using the vegetative parts of the parent plants?
modelAnswer: (a) Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; their thin walls and large surface area provide an effective surface for absorbing water and mineral salts.
Water enters the root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis because the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root hairs, often by active transport against their concentration gradient using energy.
Water and ions then move through the cortex and endodermis towards the vascular tissue of the root.
They enter the xylem, which transports water and mineral salts upwards through the plant.
(b) Artificial propagation includes techniques such as cutting, grafting and tissue culture.
In cutting, a piece of stem or root is cut from a plant and used to grow a new plant.
In grafting, a bud or small stem of one plant is attached to the roots or stems of a second plant.
Grafting enables the beneficial characteristics of two plants to be combined.
written.followUp: Explain how root hairs absorb water and mineral ions from the soil.

rubric.why: Relates the root-hair structure to absorption.
rubric.description: (a) Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; their thin walls and large surface area help them absorb water and mineral ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing root hairs and a structural feature aiding uptake.

rubric.why: Explains water uptake.
rubric.description: (a) Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis, as the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming osmosis and giving a correct explanation.

rubric.why: Explains uptake of mineral ions.
rubric.description: (a) Mineral ions may be absorbed by active transport against their concentration gradient, using energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing active uptake of mineral ions.

rubric.why: Describes the route taken by water or ions through the root.
rubric.description: (a) After entering the root, water and ions pass through the cortex and endodermis towards the vascular tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct route through the root tissues.

rubric.why: Connects root uptake to transport through the plant.
rubric.description: (a) Water and mineral salts enter the xylem and are transported upwards through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying xylem as the tissue carrying water and salts upwards.

rubric.description: (b) Name cutting, grafting and tissue culture.
rubric.why: This names the artificial propagation techniques given in the section.
rubric.how: List the three techniques.

rubric.description: (b) Describe using a cut piece of stem or root to grow a plant.
rubric.why: This explains how cutting produces a new plant.
rubric.how: Include the plant part, cutting it, and its use to grow a new plant.

rubric.description: (b) Describe attaching a bud or small stem of one plant to the roots or stems of a second plant.
rubric.why: This explains the joining action that defines grafting.
rubric.how: State what is attached and where it is attached.

rubric.description: (b) State that grafting can combine beneficial characteristics of two plants.
rubric.why: This gives an important outcome of grafting.
rubric.how: Link grafting with combining the plants' beneficial characteristics.

mcqs.stem: The hypothesis that stand the test of time are called:
rationales: Deductions are conclusions drawn from observations or premises, not tested hypotheses.
Hypotheses supported repeatedly by evidence may develop into theories.
Observations are recorded findings, not hypotheses that have stood the test of time.
Laws describe consistent patterns but are not simply hypotheses that have stood the test of time.

mcqs.stem: The Part of Earth inhibited by Organisms Communities is known as :
rationales: An ecosystem includes organisms and their interactions with the environment, not just Earth's inhabited part.
A habitat is the place where a particular organism or population lives.
The biosphere is the part of Earth inhabited by living organisms.
A population consists of members of one species living in an area.

mcqs.stem: The Function of Mitochondria is :
rationales: Mitochondria are not primarily responsible for lipid storage.
Mitochondria are the main site of cellular respiration and ATP production.
Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts, not mitochondria.
Protein synthesis occurs at ribosomes, not as the mitochondrion's main function.

mcqs.stem: In which stage of the Cell Cycle each Chromosome is duplicated and so it consist of two Chromatids:
rationales: The G1 phase is primarily a period of cell growth before DNA replication.
DNA is replicated during the S phase, producing two sister chromatids per chromosome.
The M phase is when chromosomes separate during cell division.
The G2 phase follows DNA replication and prepares the cell for division.

mcqs.stem: Which of these Tissues also called the Glandular Tissue in Animals :
rationales: Epithelial tissue includes glandular epithelium, which forms glands.
Muscular tissue is specialized for contraction, not gland secretion.
Connective tissue supports and connects body structures rather than forming glands.
Nervous tissue conducts signals rather than forming glands.

mcqs.stem: How many Carbon Atoms are in Ribose Sugar:
rationales: Six-carbon sugars include glucose, not ribose.
Ribose is a five-carbon sugar.
Four-carbon sugars are not ribose.
Three-carbon sugars are not ribose.

mcqs.stem: The Optimum Temperature for the maximum working of Human Enzyme is :
rationales: 27°C is below the optimum temperature for most human enzymes.
About 37°C is the optimum temperature for most human enzymes.
50°C is high enough to denature many human enzymes.
100°C would denature human enzymes.

mcqs.stem: The Chemical Formula of Lactic Acid is :
rationales: C₆H₁₂O₆ is the formula for glucose, not lactic acid.
C₆H₂₂O₁₁ is not the formula for lactic acid.
C₂H₂OH is not the correct molecular formula for lactic acid.
Lactic acid has the molecular formula C₃H₆O₃.

mcqs.stem: The stomata cover the leaf surface only
rationales: Stomata do not cover as much as 1–8% of the leaf surface in the stated textbook value.
Stomata do not cover as much as 1–6% of the leaf surface in the stated textbook value.
Stomata do not cover as much as 1–4% of the leaf surface in the stated textbook value.
Stomata cover only about 1–2% of the leaf surface.

mcqs.stem: Factors affecting the rate of transpiration are _____.
options: temperature, air humidity, air movement, leaf surface area
rationales: This list includes temperature, water, and light but omits key factors such as humidity and air movement.
This list includes water, light, and air movement but omits temperature and humidity.
This list includes leaf area and temperature, but sand is not a standard factor and important factors are omitted.
Temperature, air humidity, air movement, and leaf surface area all affect the rate of transpiration.

mcqs.stem: Which organism is reproduced by budding?
rationales: Amoeba usually reproduces by binary fission.
Paramecium usually reproduces by binary fission.
Sea stars can reproduce by fragmentation or regeneration, not budding as the standard example.
Hydra reproduces asexually by budding.

mcqs.stem: Sea star gains its lost arm by:
rationales: Budding is not the process by which a sea star regrows a lost arm.
Mitosis produces the new cells needed to regenerate a lost arm.
Meiosis produces reproductive cells, not replacement arm tissue.
Fragmentation is a form of reproduction and is not the process of regrowing an individual lost arm.

written.text: Define hypothesis.
modelAnswer: A hypothesis is a tentative explanation for observations or a problem.
It must be capable of being tested.
written.followUp: What is a scientific theory?

rubric.why: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation, not an established fact.
rubric.description: Identifies a hypothesis as a tentative or proposed explanation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as a tentative or proposed explanation.

rubric.why: A scientific hypothesis must be capable of testing.
rubric.description: States that a hypothesis can be tested.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning that it can be tested.

written.text: Differentiate between theory and law.
modelAnswer: A scientific law describes a consistent pattern or relationship in nature; it tells what happens.
A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation of observations; it explains how or why something happens.
written.followUp: Explain the difference between a hypothesis and a theory.

rubric.why: A scientific law describes a consistent pattern or relationship in nature.
rubric.description: Scientific law
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a law describes what happens or a regular pattern/relationship.

rubric.why: A scientific theory provides a well-supported explanation of observations and phenomena.
rubric.description: Scientific theory
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a theory explains why or how phenomena occur.

written.text: Differentiate between qualitative and quantitative observations.
modelAnswer: Qualitative observations describe qualities or characteristics and are not expressed numerically.
Quantitative observations involve measurements and are expressed in numbers.
written.followUp: Differentiate between accuracy and precision in scientific observations.

rubric.why: Qualitative observations describe qualities or characteristics without numerical measurements.
rubric.description: Meaning of qualitative observations
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that qualitative observations are descriptive or non-numerical.

rubric.why: Quantitative observations involve measurements expressed numerically.
rubric.description: Meaning of quantitative observations
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that quantitative observations involve measurements or numerical values.

written.text: What is meant by Biological Problem?
modelAnswer: A biological problem is a question about living organisms or a biological phenomenon that needs investigation.
It may arise from observations that lead to a question requiring further study.
written.followUp: What is a biological problem, and how may it arise during an investigation?

rubric.why: Defines a biological problem.
rubric.description: A biological problem is a question about living organisms or a biological phenomenon that needs investigation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an investigable question about biology.

rubric.why: Explains how a biological problem is identified.
rubric.description: It commonly arises from observations that lead to a question requiring investigation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting the problem to an observation or the need for investigation.

written.text: Define biodiversity.
modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in a particular area or on Earth.
It includes genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity.
written.followUp: Name the three levels at which biodiversity is commonly described.

rubric.why: Checks the core meaning of biodiversity.
rubric.description: Defines biodiversity as the variety of living organisms or life forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the basic definition.

rubric.why: Checks recognition of the main levels of biodiversity.
rubric.description: Mentions genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for all three levels.

written.text: Write two aims of classification.
modelAnswer: Classification groups organisms according to their similarities and differences.
It makes organisms easier to identify and study and helps show relationships among them.
written.followUp: State two reasons why classification is useful in biology.

rubric.why: Classification arranges organisms into groups based on their shared and differing features.
rubric.description: States that classification groups organisms according to similarities and differences.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this aim.

rubric.why: Classification helps with identification and study and can reveal relationships among organisms.
rubric.description: States another aim, such as facilitating identification or study, or showing relationships.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one valid additional aim.

written.text: What are plasmodesmata?
modelAnswer: Plasmodesmata are microscopic channels that pass through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells.
They connect the cells' cytoplasm and allow transport and communication between them.
written.followUp: What is the function of plasmodesmata?

rubric.why: Plasmodesmata are channels connecting neighbouring plant cells through their walls.
rubric.description: Channels connecting plant cells
rubric.how: Award for identifying them as channels or pores between adjacent plant cells.

rubric.why: These connections link the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells and allow transport or communication.
rubric.description: Connection and function
rubric.how: Award for stating that they connect the cytoplasm through the cell wall or allow transport/communication between cells.

written.text: Define facilitated diffusion.
modelAnswer: Facilitated diffusion is the passive movement of substances across a cell membrane from a higher concentration to a lower concentration.
The substances pass through channel or carrier proteins in the membrane, and no cellular energy is used.
written.followUp: What is simple diffusion, and how does it differ from facilitated diffusion?

rubric.why: Facilitated diffusion is passive movement down a concentration gradient.
rubric.description: States that substances move passively from higher to lower concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the passive, downhill movement.

rubric.why: Facilitated diffusion occurs through proteins in the cell membrane.
rubric.description: Identifies membrane channel or carrier proteins as the route of transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the membrane proteins involved.

written.text: Define Crossing Over.
modelAnswer: Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
It occurs during prophase I of meiosis.
written.followUp: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur, and between which chromatids?

rubric.why: Crossing over involves the exchange of genetic material.
rubric.description: Defines crossing over as the exchange of genetic material or chromosome segments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the exchange.

rubric.why: The exchange occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
rubric.description: Identifies the chromatids or the stage of meiosis involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes or prophase I (pachytene).

written.text: Differentiate between disjunction and non-disjunction.
modelAnswer: In disjunction, chromosomes or chromatids separate and move to opposite poles during cell division.
In nondisjunction, they fail to separate properly, producing cells with abnormal chromosome numbers.
written.followUp: What happens to chromosome number when nondisjunction occurs during meiosis?

rubric.why: Disjunction is the normal separation of chromosomes during cell division.
rubric.description: States that chromosomes or chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the normal separation.

rubric.why: Nondisjunction is a failure of normal chromosome separation and can produce cells with abnormal chromosome numbers.
rubric.description: States that chromosomes fail to separate, causing abnormal chromosome numbers in the resulting cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the failure to separate and its consequence.

written.text: Define population.
modelAnswer: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
written.followUp: Define a community and give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies the organisms and the shared place and time that define a population.
rubric.description: A group of individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including same species and a shared area or habitat; the definition must also indicate that the organisms live there together (at the same time).

rubric.why: Recognizes the ecological term being defined.
rubric.description: Correctly identifies the group as a population.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the group a population.

written.text: Define population and community.
modelAnswer: A population is a group of organisms of the same species living in a particular area.
A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
written.followUp: What is a population? Give one example of a population in an ecosystem.

rubric.why: A population is made up of organisms belonging to the same species in a defined area.
rubric.description: Defines population.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including organisms of the same species living in the same area.

rubric.why: A community includes populations of different species living and interacting in a shared area.
rubric.description: Defines community.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including populations of different species in a shared area or their interactions.

written.text: What are Bioelements?
modelAnswer: Bioelements are the elements that are present in living organisms.
Examples include carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.
written.followUp: What are the major bioelements, and name four elements found in living organisms?

rubric.why: Bioelements are the elements present in living organisms.
rubric.description: Defines bioelements.
rubric.how: Award for stating that bioelements are elements present in living organisms.

rubric.why: Examples demonstrate understanding of which elements are bioelements.
rubric.description: Provides examples of bioelements.
rubric.how: Award for naming at least two valid examples, such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen or nitrogen.

written.text: Write any four sources of lipids.
modelAnswer: Four sources of lipids are butter, ghee, vegetable oils, and nuts.
written.followUp: Name four foods that are good sources of proteins.

rubric.why: Recognises animal-derived sources of lipids.
rubric.description: Names two animal sources of lipids.
rubric.how: Award the mark for any two correct animal sources, such as butter, ghee, milk, or egg yolk.

rubric.why: Recognises plant-derived sources of lipids.
rubric.description: Names two plant sources of lipids.
rubric.how: Award the mark for any two correct plant sources, such as vegetable oils, nuts, or seeds.

written.text: Define double fertilization. Give its outcome.
modelAnswer: Double fertilization is the occurrence of two fusion events in the embryo sac of a flowering plant.
One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a zygote, while the other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm.
written.followUp: Explain what happens to the two male gametes during fertilization in a flowering plant.

rubric.why: Double fertilization is defined by two fusion events occurring in the embryo sac of a flowering plant.
rubric.description: Definition of double fertilization
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two fusion events occur in the embryo sac.

rubric.why: The two fusion events result in the formation of a zygote and endosperm.
rubric.description: Outcome of double fertilization
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both the zygote and endosperm as outcomes.

written.text: Compare bulb with corm.
modelAnswer: A bulb has a short stem surrounded by fleshy scale leaves that store food; onion is an example.
A corm is a solid, swollen underground stem covered with dry scale leaves; gladiolus is an example.
written.followUp: Compare a rhizome with a tuber.

rubric.why: A bulb has a short stem with fleshy scale leaves that store food; onion is an example.
rubric.description: Feature of a bulb
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct distinguishing feature or example of a bulb.

rubric.why: A corm is a solid, swollen underground stem, usually covered by dry scale leaves; gladiolus and colocasia are examples.
rubric.description: Feature of a corm
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct distinguishing feature or example of a corm.

written.text: How enzymes lower the activation energy?
modelAnswer: An enzyme binds its substrate to form an enzyme substrate complex and provides a pathway with a lower energy barrier.
Thus, less activation energy is needed for the reaction to occur.
written.followUp: What is activation energy, and how does an enzyme affect it?

rubric.why: Checks the mechanism by which an enzyme helps a reaction proceed.
rubric.description: States that an enzyme forms an enzyme-substrate complex or provides an alternative pathway.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either key mechanism.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of the enzyme on the reaction's energy barrier.
rubric.description: States that enzymes lower the activation energy needed for the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explicitly stating that activation energy is reduced.

written.text: Differentiate between intracellular enzymes and extra cellular enzymes.
modelAnswer: Intracellular enzymes remain and act inside the cell, for example enzymes involved in cellular respiration.
Extracellular enzymes are secreted by cells and act outside the cell, for example digestive enzymes acting in the gut.
written.followUp: Give one example of an extracellular enzyme and state where it acts.

rubric.why: Intracellular enzymes carry out their reactions inside cells.
rubric.description: Distinguishes intracellular enzymes by their site of action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that intracellular enzymes act inside the cell.

rubric.why: Extracellular enzymes are released from cells and act outside them.
rubric.description: Distinguishes extracellular enzymes by their site of action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that extracellular enzymes are secreted and act outside the cell.

written.text: Define cellular respiration.
modelAnswer: Cellular respiration is the process in which cells break down food molecules, especially glucose.
Energy is released and captured in ATP for the cell’s activities.
written.followUp: What is the main energy-storing product of cellular respiration?

rubric.why: Identifies the breakdown of food, especially glucose, as the process of respiration.
rubric.description: Defines cellular respiration as the breakdown of food molecules in cells.
rubric.how: Award for stating that cells break down food or glucose during cellular respiration.

rubric.why: States the outcome of respiration for the cell.
rubric.description: Explains that respiration releases energy, which is captured in ATP.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning released energy and its capture or storage in ATP.

written.text: What is Glycolysis?
modelAnswer: Glycolysis is the series of reactions in which one glucose molecule is broken down into two molecules of pyruvic acid.
It takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell.
written.followUp: Where does glycolysis occur, and what is its main product?

rubric.why: Awards the central change in glycolysis.
rubric.description: States that glucose is broken down to pyruvic acid (pyruvate).
rubric.how: Check for glucose as the starting molecule and pyruvic acid or pyruvate as the product.

rubric.why: Awards the cellular location of glycolysis.
rubric.description: States that glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Check for cytoplasm or cytosol.

written.text: What is meant by Electron Transport Chain?
modelAnswer: The electron transport chain is a series of electron carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Electrons pass from one carrier to another and finally to oxygen; the released energy is used to produce ATP.
written.followUp: What is the role of oxygen at the end of the electron transport chain?

rubric.why: Identifies the electron transport chain and its location.
rubric.description: The electron transport chain is a series of electron carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a carrier chain and its mitochondrial location.

rubric.why: Explains electron transfer and its connection to ATP formation.
rubric.description: Electrons pass along the carriers to oxygen; the released energy is used to make ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for electron transfer to oxygen and/or the resulting energy being used to form ATP.

written.text: Why transpiration is necessary for plants?
modelAnswer: Transpiration creates a pull that helps transport water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves.
It also cools the plant.
written.followUp: Describe one role of transpiration in the upward movement of water in plants.

rubric.why: Water loss from leaves creates a pull that helps move water upward through the plant.
rubric.description: States that transpiration creates a pull.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning transpiration pull.

rubric.why: Transpiration supports the movement of water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves.
rubric.description: Links transpiration to the transport of water, with minerals, through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking transpiration to water or mineral transport.

written.text: What is “Cohesion-Tension Theory”?
modelAnswer: The cohesion-tension theory states that transpiration from leaves creates tension in the xylem, pulling water upward.
Cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous column of water from the roots to the leaves.
written.followUp: How does transpiration pull help water move up through xylem?

rubric.why: Transpiration from leaves creates tension that pulls water upward through the xylem.
rubric.description: States that transpiration creates tension or a pull in the xylem.
rubric.how: Award for identifying transpiration as the source of the upward pulling force.

rubric.why: Cohesion between water molecules keeps the water column continuous as it is pulled upward.
rubric.description: Explains how cohesion maintains the water column.
rubric.how: Award for linking cohesion to a continuous water column.

written.text: Differentiate between Cohesion and Adhesion.
modelAnswer: Cohesion is the attraction between molecules of the same substance, such as water molecules attracting one another.
Adhesion is the attraction between molecules of different substances, such as water molecules attracting the walls of a xylem vessel.
written.followUp: Differentiate between transpiration and evaporation.

rubric.why: Cohesion is attraction between molecules of the same substance.
rubric.description: Defines cohesion as attraction between molecules of the same substance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the attraction as occurring between like molecules.

rubric.why: Adhesion is attraction between molecules of different substances.
rubric.description: Defines adhesion as attraction between molecules of different substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the attraction as occurring between unlike substances.

written.text:
(a) Define endangered species. Give reasons of endangerment of the species found in Pakistan.
(b) Write four benefits of electron microscope.
modelAnswer: (a) An endangered species is a species whose population has fallen to such a low level that it is at risk of extinction.
In Pakistan, habitat destruction and deforestation reduce the food, shelter and breeding sites available to wildlife.
Illegal hunting and poaching directly reduce the populations of animals such as markhor and snow leopard.
Pollution and other human activities also damage habitats and threaten species, including aquatic wildlife such as the Indus dolphin.
(b) An electron microscope provides much higher magnification than a light microscope.
Its greater resolving power reveals finer details.
It can be used to observe very small objects such as viruses.
It shows the fine structure of cells and their organelles.
written.followUp: Define an endangered species and describe two ways its habitat can be protected in Pakistan.

rubric.why: An endangered species has a population so low that it is at risk of extinction.
rubric.description: (a) Defines an endangered species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the species is threatened with extinction or has very low numbers and may become extinct.

rubric.why: Destruction or loss of habitat reduces the places where species can live and reproduce.
rubric.description: (a) Explains habitat destruction as a cause of endangerment.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for identifying habitat loss or deforestation and linking it to declining populations.

rubric.why: Hunting, pollution and other human pressures can further reduce wildlife populations in Pakistan.
rubric.description: (a) Gives other causes of endangerment.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for two further valid causes, or one cause explained clearly.

rubric.why: Electron microscopes can magnify much more than light microscopes.
rubric.description: (b) States that an electron microscope provides higher magnification.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its greater magnifying power.

rubric.why: Greater resolving power allows finer details to be distinguished.
rubric.description: (b) Mentions the electron microscope’s resolving power or its ability to show finer details.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it can distinguish details that a light microscope cannot.

rubric.why: Electron microscopes can be used to observe objects too small to see with a light microscope, such as viruses.
rubric.description: (b) Gives viruses or another suitable example of a very small object that can be observed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example.

rubric.why: Its magnification and resolution allow fine cellular structures to be studied.
rubric.description: (b) Mentions observing fine cell structure or organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the study of cell ultrastructure or organelles.

written.text:
(a) Define vitamins and discuss vitamin A and vitamin C in detail.
(b) Describe the use of Enzymes in different Industries.
modelAnswer: (a) Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts for normal growth and health.
Vitamin A is needed for normal vision and healthy epithelial tissues; deficiency may cause night-blindness.
Sources of vitamin A include carrots, milk, eggs and fish-liver oil.
Vitamin C is needed for collagen formation and wound healing; its deficiency causes scurvy, which may include bleeding gums.
Citrus fruits and fresh vegetables are sources of vitamin C.
(b) Enzymes are used in detergents to break down stains and improve cleaning.
In the food industry, enzymes are used in cheese-making, baking and fruit-juice processing.
In the textile industry, enzymes help process and finish fabrics.
In the leather industry, enzymes help remove hair from hides or soften leather.
written.followUp: Compare vitamins D and B₁ by giving a function, a source and a deficiency effect for each.

rubric.why: Provides a correct definition of vitamins.
rubric.description: (a) Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts for normal growth and health.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing vitamins as organic compounds needed in small quantities.

rubric.why: States an important function or deficiency effect of vitamin A.
rubric.description: (a) Vitamin A is needed for normal vision; its deficiency can cause night-blindness.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct vitamin A function or deficiency effect.

rubric.why: Names a valid source of vitamin A.
rubric.description: (a) Sources include carrots, milk, eggs and fish-liver oil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid vitamin A source.

rubric.why: States an important function or deficiency effect of vitamin C.
rubric.description: (a) Vitamin C supports collagen formation and wound healing; its deficiency causes scurvy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct vitamin C function or deficiency effect.

rubric.why: Names a valid source of vitamin C.
rubric.description: (a) Citrus fruits and fresh vegetables are sources of vitamin C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid vitamin C source.

rubric.why: Credits a correct use of enzymes in detergents.
rubric.description: (b) Enzymes in detergents break down stains and improve cleaning.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct detergent application.

rubric.why: Credits examples of enzyme use in food processing.
rubric.description: (b) Enzymes are used in food processing, including cheese-making, baking and fruit-juice processing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least one valid food-industry use.

rubric.why: Credits a correct textile-industry application.
rubric.description: (b) Enzymes help process or finish fabrics in the textile industry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid textile application.

rubric.why: Credits a correct leather-industry application.
rubric.description: (b) Enzymes are used to remove hair from hides or soften leather.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid leather application.

written.text:
(a) How transport of water takes place in plants ?
(b) Define sporophyte and gametophyte. State their roles in the life cycle of plants.
modelAnswer: (a) Root hairs absorb water from the soil, mainly by osmosis.
Water passes across the root cortex and enters the xylem.
Xylem vessels carry water and dissolved mineral salts upward through the stem to the leaves.
Transpiration from leaves creates a pull that draws the water column upward.
Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls help keep the column continuous; root pressure may also assist.
(b) The diploid generation that produces spores is called the sporophyte generation.
The haploid generation that produces gametes is called the gametophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces spores, which grow into the gametophyte generation.
The gametophyte produces gametes, which unite to form a zygote that develops into the next sporophyte.
written.followUp: Describe how minerals dissolved in soil water reach the leaves of a plant.

rubric.why: Describes the entry of water into the plant.
rubric.description: (a) Root hairs absorb water from the soil, mainly by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming root hairs and water absorption (osmosis where specified).

rubric.why: Shows the route water takes through the root to reach the conducting tissue.
rubric.description: (a) Water passes through the root cortex and enters the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing passage through the root to the xylem.

rubric.why: Identifies the tissue that carries water upward through the plant.
rubric.description: (a) Water and dissolved minerals move upward through xylem vessels in the stem to the leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying xylem as the transport tissue.

rubric.why: Explains the forces responsible for the upward movement of water.
rubric.description: (a) Transpiration pull is the main force; cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls help maintain the water column. Root pressure may also assist.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for explaining transpiration pull and at least one supporting force or mechanism.

rubric.description: (b) Defines the sporophyte generation.
rubric.why: The ploidy and product define the sporophyte.
rubric.how: State that the diploid sporophyte produces spores.

rubric.description: (b) Defines the gametophyte generation.
rubric.why: The ploidy and product define the gametophyte.
rubric.how: State that the haploid gametophyte produces gametes.

rubric.description: (b) Explains how spores form the gametophyte.
rubric.why: This explains how one generation gives rise to the next.
rubric.how: Say spores grow into the gametophyte generation.

rubric.description: (b) Explains how gametes lead to a new sporophyte.
rubric.why: This completes the cycle by explaining how gametes lead to a new sporophyte.
rubric.how: Say gametes unite to form a zygote, which develops into the sporophyte.

mcqs.stem: The Logical Consequences of Hypothesis is called :
rationales: Observations are recorded findings, not the logical consequences derived from a hypothesis.
A deduction is a logical consequence derived from a hypothesis.
Experiments test a hypothesis or its predictions rather than name the logical consequences.
A theory is a broad explanation supported by evidence, not a prediction from a hypothesis.

mcqs.stem: All the Members of which group are Absorptive in their Nutrition:
rationales: Protists have varied modes of nutrition, so not all are absorptive.
Animals obtain food by ingestion rather than absorption across their body surface.
Bacteria include both autotrophs and heterotrophs, so not all are absorptive.
Fungi obtain nutrients by absorption, making this the correct group.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following Organelles is without Membrane:
rationales: A mitochondrion is surrounded by membranes.
A chloroplast is surrounded by membranes.
A ribosome is not surrounded by a membrane.
A lysosome is enclosed by a membrane.

mcqs.stem: What is the time required for the completion of interphase during cell cycle?
rationales: Interphase takes substantially more than 60% of the cell cycle.
Interphase takes substantially more than 70% of the cell cycle.
Interphase takes substantially more than 80% of the cell cycle.
Interphase occupies about 90% of the cell cycle.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following contain Deoxygenated Blood in an Adult Human :
rationales: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.
The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
The left atrium contains oxygenated blood returning from the lungs.
The left ventricle contains oxygenated blood that is pumped to the body.

mcqs.stem: Which of these major bioelements is in the lowest percentage in protoplasm?
rationales: Carbon is present in protoplasm in a greater proportion than nitrogen.
Hydrogen is present in protoplasm in a greater proportion than nitrogen.
Oxygen is the most abundant of these bioelements in protoplasm.
Nitrogen has the lowest percentage among these major bioelements in protoplasm.

mcqs.stem: Enzyme used for the Removal of Protein Stains from Clothes is called:
rationales: Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach but is not the general answer for laundry stain removal.
Amylase breaks down starch, not protein stains.
Protease enzymes break down proteins and are used to remove protein stains.
Lipase breaks down fats, not protein stains.

mcqs.stem: Which of these can Enter into Krebs Cycle :
rationales: Acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate to enter the Krebs cycle.
Citric acid is formed within the Krebs cycle rather than being the usual entry substrate.
Pyruvic acid is converted to acetyl CoA before entering the Krebs cycle.
Glucose is broken down through glycolysis before its products enter the Krebs cycle.

mcqs.stem: _____ of plant is responsible for the flow of water.
rationales: Leaves are not the plant tissue that conducts water through the plant.
Phloem transports sugars and other organic substances, not water as its main function.
Roots absorb water, but do not conduct it throughout the plant.
Xylem conducts water through the plant.

mcqs.stem: Which element regulates the opening and closing of stomata:
rationales: Sulphur is not the element that regulates stomatal opening and closing.
Potassium regulates the opening and closing of stomata.
Calcium is not the expected answer for stomatal regulation in this question.
Phosphorus does not regulate stomatal opening and closing.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following organisms commonly reproduce by binary fission?
rationales: Yeast commonly reproduces by budding rather than binary fission.
Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission.
Rhizopus commonly reproduces by spores rather than binary fission.
Plants generally reproduce sexually or by vegetative propagation, not by binary fission.

mcqs.stem: What is the primary method of reproduction in yeast?
rationales: Binary fission is not the primary method of reproduction in yeast.
Spore formation occurs in some fungi but is not yeast’s primary method of reproduction.
Yeast primarily reproduces asexually by budding.
Fragmentation is not the primary method of reproduction in yeast.

written.text: What are deductions?
modelAnswer: Deductions are logical conclusions drawn from observations, often using prior knowledge.
written.followUp: What is a hypothesis?

rubric.why: Deductions are logical conclusions or inferences drawn from observations, often using prior knowledge.
rubric.description: Defines deductions.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for defining deductions as conclusions or inferences drawn from observations; award 1 mark for mentioning a conclusion or inference without linking it to observations.

written.text: What are quantitative observations? Give example.
modelAnswer: Quantitative observations are observations expressed as numbers or measurements.
Example: a plant is 10 cm tall.
written.followUp: What are qualitative observations? Give one example.

rubric.why: Explains that quantitative observations use measurements or numerical data.
rubric.description: Quantitative observations are observations expressed in numbers or measurements.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning numerical or measured data.

rubric.why: Provides a suitable numerical example of a measured observation.
rubric.description: Example: a plant is 10 cm tall.
rubric.how: Award for a relevant example that includes a quantity or measurement.

written.text: Write two characteristics of a good hypothesis.
modelAnswer: A good hypothesis is clearly stated and based on observations.
It must be testable by observation or experiment.
written.followUp: Write two characteristics of a good scientific experiment.

rubric.why: A hypothesis must be capable of being tested.
rubric.description: States that a good hypothesis is testable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying testability.

rubric.why: A good hypothesis should be clearly expressed and grounded in observations or a prediction.
rubric.description: Gives another valid characteristic of a good hypothesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one relevant characteristic apart from testability.

written.text: Define deduction.
modelAnswer: Deduction is a process of reasoning in which a particular conclusion is drawn from a general principle or statement.
written.followUp: What is induction in the biological method?

rubric.why: Checks the direction and nature of deductive reasoning.
rubric.description: Defines deduction as reasoning from a general principle to a particular conclusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying reasoning or drawing a conclusion, and 1 mark for stating the general-to-particular direction.

written.text: Differentiate between Prions and Viroids.
modelAnswer: Prions are infectious protein particles and do not contain nucleic acid.
Viroids are small infectious RNA molecules without a protein coat; they mainly infect plants.
written.followUp: Differentiate between bacteria and viruses.

rubric.why: Identifies the composition of prions.
rubric.description: Prions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that prions are infectious protein particles and lack nucleic acid.

rubric.why: Identifies the composition or host of viroids.
rubric.description: Viroids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viroids are small infectious RNA molecules without a protein coat, commonly infecting plants.

written.text: Define systematics.
modelAnswer: Systematics is the study of the diversity of organisms and their relationships.
written.followUp: What does systematics study besides the diversity of organisms?

rubric.why: Identifies the diversity or variety of organisms as part of systematics.
rubric.description: States that systematics studies the diversity of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning organismal diversity or variety.

rubric.why: Includes the relationships among organisms, another central part of systematics.
rubric.description: States that systematics studies relationships among organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning relationships among organisms.

written.text: What is plasmodesmata?
modelAnswer: Plasmodesmata are narrow cytoplasmic channels that pass through the cell walls of neighbouring plant cells.
They connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells and allow transport and communication between them.
written.followUp: What are the functions of plasmodesmata in plant cells?

rubric.why: Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels passing through the walls between neighbouring plant cells.
rubric.description: Structure of plasmodesmata
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as channels connecting the cytoplasm of adjacent plant cells through their walls.

rubric.why: These connections enable substances and signals to pass between neighbouring cells.
rubric.description: Function of plasmodesmata
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they facilitate transport or communication between adjacent cells.

written.text: Differentiate between cell membrane and plasma membrane.
modelAnswer: Cell membrane and plasma membrane are two names for the same structure, not two different membranes.
This membrane is selectively permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
written.followUp: State one similarity and one difference between the cell wall and the plasma membrane.

rubric.why: Cell membrane and plasma membrane are names for the same cell boundary.
rubric.description: Identifies the terms as referring to the same structure, not two different membranes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the terms are equivalent.

rubric.why: Selective permeability and regulation of movement are key features of this membrane.
rubric.description: States that the membrane is selectively permeable or controls movement of substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a correct property or function.

written.text: Define chiasmata.
modelAnswer: Chiasmata are the visible points where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes remain attached after crossing over during meiosis.
written.followUp: During which stage of meiosis do chiasmata become visible?

rubric.why: Chiasmata mark sites where crossing over has occurred between homologous chromosomes.
rubric.description: Connects chiasmata with crossing over or genetic-material exchange.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning crossing over or exchange between chromatids.

rubric.why: Chiasmata occur between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
rubric.description: Identifies the chromosome chromatids involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.

written.text: What is meant by metastasis?
modelAnswer: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the original tumour to other parts of the body, often through the blood or lymph.
These cells may form secondary tumours at the new locations.
written.followUp: How do cancer cells form secondary tumours in other parts of the body?

rubric.why: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells away from the original tumour.
rubric.description: Spread from the original tumour
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that cancer cells spread from the original tumour.

rubric.why: Metastasis can result in secondary tumours at other locations.
rubric.description: Secondary tumours elsewhere
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the spread can form secondary or new tumours in other parts of the body.

written.text: What do you know about appendix?
modelAnswer: The appendix is a small, narrow, finger-like projection attached to the caecum of the large intestine.
It is considered vestigial, and its inflammation is called appendicitis.
written.followUp: Where is the appendix located, and what is appendicitis?

rubric.why: Identifies the appendix’s anatomical attachment.
rubric.description: The appendix is a small, narrow, finger-like projection attached to the caecum.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the caecum as the structure to which the appendix is attached.

rubric.why: Gives a relevant fact about the appendix and its inflammation.
rubric.description: The appendix is considered vestigial; its inflammation is called appendicitis.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it is vestigial or that its inflammation is called appendicitis.

written.text: Differentiate between thrombus and embolus.
modelAnswer: A thrombus is a blood clot formed in a blood vessel that remains attached at its place of formation.
An embolus is a detached clot or other material that travels through the bloodstream.
written.followUp: Differentiate between an artery and a vein.

rubric.why: Identifies the thrombus as a clot that stays at its site of formation.
rubric.description: A thrombus is a blood clot formed in a blood vessel that remains at its place of formation.
rubric.how: Award for identifying it as a clot and stating that it remains attached or at its place of formation.

rubric.why: Identifies the embolus as material that has detached and is moving in the circulation.
rubric.description: An embolus is a detached clot or other material that travels through the bloodstream.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it is detached and travels through the bloodstream.

written.text: What are causes and symptoms of Kwashiorkor?
modelAnswer: Kwashiorkor is caused mainly by a severe deficiency of protein in the diet, often after a child is weaned.
Symptoms include edema (swelling), a swollen abdomen, stunted growth, and changes in hair or skin.
written.followUp: What causes marasmus, and name one of its symptoms.

rubric.why: Kwashiorkor is caused mainly by an inadequate protein intake, often after weaning.
rubric.description: States the dietary cause of Kwashiorkor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protein deficiency or inadequate protein in the diet.

rubric.why: These are characteristic symptoms of Kwashiorkor.
rubric.description: Names one symptom of Kwashiorkor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any valid symptom.

written.text: Differentiate between micromolecules and macromolecules with examples.
modelAnswer: Micromolecules are small molecules with low molecular mass, for example glucose or amino acids.
Macromolecules are large molecules with high molecular mass, for example proteins or starch.
written.followUp: Differentiate between organic and inorganic compounds in cells, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Micromolecules are small molecules with low molecular mass; glucose, amino acids and water are examples.
rubric.description: Micromolecules
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying micromolecules as small or low-molecular-mass molecules and giving a suitable example.

rubric.why: Macromolecules are large molecules with high molecular mass; proteins, starch, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are examples.
rubric.description: Macromolecules
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying macromolecules as large or high-molecular-mass molecules and giving a suitable example.

written.text: What is Binary fission?
modelAnswer: Binary fission is a type of asexual reproduction involving one parent.
The parent cell divides to form two daughter cells.
written.followUp: How does binary fission differ from budding?

rubric.why: Identifies the type of reproduction and parent involved.
rubric.description: Binary fission is a form of asexual reproduction involving one parent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as asexual reproduction or stating that it involves one parent.

rubric.why: Describes the defining outcome of binary fission.
rubric.description: The parent cell divides to form two daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one cell divides into two daughter cells.

written.text: Differentiate between vegetative and reproductive parts of mustard plant.
modelAnswer: The vegetative parts of mustard are the roots, stem and leaves.
The reproductive parts are the flowers, fruits (pods) and seeds.
written.followUp: Name the vegetative and reproductive parts of a pea plant.

rubric.why: Roots, stems and leaves perform vegetative functions.
rubric.description: Names the vegetative parts of mustard.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the roots, stem and leaves.

rubric.why: Flowers, fruits and seeds are involved in reproduction.
rubric.description: Names the reproductive parts of mustard.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the flowers, fruits (pods) and seeds.

written.text: What is difference between pepsin and pepsinogen?
modelAnswer: Pepsin is the active protein-digesting enzyme in the stomach.
Pepsinogen is its inactive precursor; hydrochloric acid activates it to form pepsin.
written.followUp: Differentiate between trypsin and trypsinogen.

rubric.why: Distinguishes pepsin as the active enzyme.
rubric.description: Pepsin is the active form of the enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying pepsin as active.

rubric.why: Distinguishes pepsinogen as the inactive form that becomes pepsin.
rubric.description: Pepsinogen is an inactive precursor that is activated by hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying pepsinogen as inactive or as the precursor of pepsin.

written.text: What is meant by optimum temperature?
modelAnswer: The optimum temperature is the temperature at which an enzyme catalyses a reaction at its maximum rate.
written.followUp: What is the optimum pH of an enzyme?

rubric.why: The optimum temperature is the temperature at which an enzyme works at its highest rate.
rubric.description: Defines optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award for linking the temperature to maximum or fastest enzyme activity.

written.text: What is meant by lactic acid fermentation?
modelAnswer: Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose in which lactic acid is produced.
It can occur in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient and in some bacteria.
written.followUp: What is alcoholic fermentation, and under what conditions does it occur?

rubric.why: Lactic acid fermentation is an anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.description: Identifies the process as anaerobic glucose breakdown.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen.

rubric.why: The process forms lactic acid and may occur in muscle cells or certain bacteria.
rubric.description: Names the product or a valid site of lactic acid fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming lactic acid as the product or giving a valid example such as muscles or bacteria.

written.text: Define lactic acid fermentation.
modelAnswer: Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to form lactic acid.
It releases only a small amount of energy.
written.followUp: Define alcoholic fermentation.

written.text:
(a) How would you explain the structure and functions of compound tissues?
(b) Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.
modelAnswer: (a) Compound tissues consist of different types of cells that work together to perform a common function.
Xylem is made up of vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots towards the leaves and also provides support.
Phloem is made up of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
Phloem transports (translocates) food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.
(b) The ovule acts as a megasporangium and contains a diploid megaspore mother cell.
The megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores.
Only one megaspore remains alive.
Inside the megaspore, mitosis forms eight haploid nuclei.
Two nuclei migrate to the centre and fuse to form a fusion nucleus.
One nucleus out of the remaining six forms the egg cell.
The resulting embryo sac has seven cells: one egg cell, one fusion nucleus, and five non-functional cells.

written.text: Describe the work of different scientists in discovering the cause of malaria.
modelAnswer: In 1878, Laveran examined the blood of a malarial patient and noticed microorganisms, which were named Plasmodium.
Biologists suggested the hypothesis: “Plasmodium is the cause of malaria”.
A. F. A. King suggested the hypothesis: “Mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium and so are involved in the spread of malaria.”
Ronald Ross allowed female Culex mosquitoes to bite a sparrow suffering from malaria.
He found that Plasmodium multiplied in the walls of the mosquito’s stomach and then moved into its salivary glands.
He allowed infected mosquitoes to bite healthy sparrows, which got malaria.
In 1898, Italian biologists allowed an infected Anopheles mosquito to bite a healthy man, who later became ill with malaria.

Ross allowed infected mosquitoes to bite healthy sparrows.

written.text: What is Binomial Nomenclature. Give its rules
modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of naming each organism with a two-word scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name.
The names are Latin or Latinised.
In print, both words are italicised; when handwritten, they are underlined separately.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, while the species name begins with a lowercase letter; for example, *Homo sapiens*.

written.text: Write in detail the importance of biodiversity with respect to natural ecosystem with an example.
modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an ecosystem, and it helps maintain ecosystem balance and stability.
Different species are linked in food chains and food webs, so changes in one population can affect others.
A variety of organisms also supports essential processes such as nutrient cycling.
Biodiverse ecosystems are generally more resilient and can better withstand or recover from environmental changes.
For example, in a forest, many plant and animal species form food webs; insects pollinate plants, while decomposers recycle nutrients.

written.text:
(a) Write in detail the importance of biodiversity with respect to natural ecosystem with an example.
(b) Define binomial nomenclature and write its rules.
modelAnswer: (a) Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an ecosystem, and it helps maintain ecosystem balance and stability.
Different species are linked in food chains and food webs, so changes in one population can affect others.
A variety of organisms also supports essential processes such as nutrient cycling.
Biodiverse ecosystems are generally more resilient and can better withstand or recover from environmental changes.
For example, in a forest, many plant and animal species form food webs; insects pollinate plants, while decomposers recycle nutrients.
(b) Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a scientific name consisting of two words.
The first word is the genus name and begins with a capital letter.
The second word is the species name and begins with a lowercase letter.
The two words are italicized in print; when handwritten, they are underlined separately.

written.text: Explain Active Transport.
modelAnswer: Active transport is the movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, from a lower concentration to a higher concentration.
It requires energy, usually supplied as ATP during respiration.
Carrier or transport proteins in the cell membrane assist in moving the substances.
For example, root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, even when their concentration is lower in the soil than in the cells.
Active transport is selective and also helps cells absorb substances such as glucose and amino acids.

written.text: Define disjunction and non-disjunction.
modelAnswer: Disjunction is the normal separation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis.
Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis, resulting in cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes.

written.text: What is meant by Apoptotic Bodies?
modelAnswer: During apoptosis, the cell breaks into small membrane bound fragments called apoptotic bodies.
These bodies are engulfed by neighbouring cells or phagocytes.
written.followUp: What happens to a cell during apoptosis?

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their removal.

written.text: What is the difference between somatic cells and germ line cells?
modelAnswer: Somatic cells are the ordinary body cells and are not directly involved in producing gametes.
Germ-line cells are reproductive cells that give rise to gametes through meiosis; somatic cells divide by mitosis.

rubric.why: The cell types differ in their division and relationship to gamete formation.
rubric.description: Gives a correct difference in division or chromosome number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that somatic cells divide by mitosis while germ-line cells form gametes by meiosis, or for a correct chromosome-number contrast.

written.text: What is synapsis?
modelAnswer: Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes.
It occurs during prophase I of meiosis, specifically in zygotene.

written.text: Define karyokinesis.
modelAnswer: Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus during cell division.

written.text: Differentiate between apoptosis and necrosis.
modelAnswer: Apoptosis is programmed and controlled cell death.
Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death that occurs due to injury or damage.

written.text: What is difference between karyokinesis and cytokinesis?
modelAnswer: Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus.

written.text: How cytokinesis takes place in plant cells?

The cell plate grows towards the periphery and joins the cell boundary, dividing the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.

written.text: What is chiasmata?
modelAnswer: Chiasmata are the points where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes cross over and exchange genetic material.
They form during prophase I of meiosis.

written.text: Define cytokinesis.

written.text: What is kinetochore?
modelAnswer: A kinetochore is a protein structure formed at the centromere of a chromosome.

written.text: When and who discovered meiosis?

written.text: What is difference between benign and malignant tumors?
modelAnswer: A benign tumour is non-cancerous and remains localized; it does not invade nearby tissues.
A malignant tumour is cancerous, invades surrounding tissues and may spread to other parts of the body.

rubric.why: Malignant tumours invade nearby tissues and can spread to distant parts of the body.
rubric.description: Describes malignant tumours as invasive or able to spread.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct distinguishing feature of malignant tumours.

written.text: What is phragmoplast? Give its function.
modelAnswer: A phragmoplast is a group of microtubules that forms between the daughter nuclei in a dividing plant cell.
It guides the formation of the cell plate during cytokinesis.

written.text: What is tumor? Write their types.
modelAnswer: A tumour is an abnormal mass of cells formed as a result of uncontrolled cell division.

written.text: How the Meiosis is Beneficial for Next Generation?
modelAnswer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces haploid gametes.
At fertilization, two haploid gametes fuse and restore the diploid chromosome number.
Thus, the chromosome number remains constant from one generation to the next.

written.text: Describe the G2 Phase of Cell Cycle.
modelAnswer: G2 is the second gap phase; it occurs after DNA replication (S phase) and before mitosis.

modelAnswer: During prophase I of meiosis, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes pair up.
They exchange corresponding segments of genetic material at points called chiasmata.
This exchange forms new gene combinations and increases genetic variation.

written.text: Compare Sister Chromatids and Non-Sister Chromatids.
modelAnswer: Sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome joined together at the centromere.

modelAnswer: In the G₀ phase, a cell leaves the active cell cycle and does not divide.

written.text: Define tumors. How they formed?

written.text: How disjunction is different from non-disjunction? (1+1)
modelAnswer: In disjunction, homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids separate normally during cell division.

written.text: What is phragmoplast? Why is it important for plant cell? (1+1)
modelAnswer: A phragmoplast is a structure of microtubules that forms between the daughter nuclei during cytokinesis in a plant cell.

written.text: What do you know about the process of disjunction and non-disjunction?
modelAnswer: Disjunction is the normal separation of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids during meiosis.

written.text: What is cell cycle and what are its main phases?
modelAnswer: The cell cycle is the series of events through which a cell grows and divides to form two daughter cells.
Its two main phases are interphase and the mitotic phase (M phase).
During interphase, the cell grows and replicates its DNA; during the mitotic phase, the cell divides.

written.text: Write down the role of mitosis in regeneration.
modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells at the site of injury or loss.
These cells replace damaged or lost cells and help regenerate the body part.

written.text: What are blebs and apoptotic bodies?
modelAnswer: Blebs are bubble-like bulges that form on the cell membrane during apoptosis.
Apoptotic bodies are membrane-enclosed fragments of the dying cell; they are engulfed by other cells.

written.text: What are changes take place during anaphase I?

modelAnswer: Golgi-derived vesicles gather at the equator of the plant cell and fuse to form a cell plate.

written.text: Why mitosis does not occur in prokaryotes?
modelAnswer: Mitosis is nuclear division, but prokaryotes do not have a nucleus.

written.text: How cytokinesis occur in animal cells?
modelAnswer: The plasma membrane of an animal cell constricts inward, forming a cleavage furrow.
