written.text:
(a) Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
(b) Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
modelAnswer: (a) Karyokinesis means division of the nucleus and is divided into four phases.
During prophase, thread-like chromatin condenses and makes thick visible chromosomes.
The nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down, and spindle fibres form.
During metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres at the centromere and arrange along the equator, forming the metaphase plate.
During anaphase, spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids apart towards opposite poles.
During telophase, a new nuclear envelope forms around each set, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and results in two daughter cells.
(b) In prophase-I, chromatin condenses into chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis to form tetrads.
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids, exchanging portions of chromosomes.
In metaphase-I, tetrads attached to spindle fibres align along the equator and form the metaphase plate.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate; one chromosome from each pair moves toward each opposite pole. Each chromosome still contains two sister chromatids.
In telophase-I, spindles disappear, nuclear envelopes and nucleoli reform, and chromosomes uncoil into chromatin.
Cytokinesis occurs, producing two haploid daughter cells.

written.text:
(a) Describe the significance of mitosis.
(b) Describe the significance of meiosis.
modelAnswer: (a) Growth occurs due to an increase in the number of cells.
Mitosis produces new cells that are identical to the original cells and plays a crucial role in growth.
Many cells constantly die in the body; mitosis forms new cells that are exact copies of the older cells to replace them.
Some animals regenerate parts of the body by forming new cells through mitosis in the cells of the remaining parts.
Mitosis is a means for asexual reproduction; for example, in Hydra it forms a bud that grows into a new individual.
(b) In animals, meiosis produces gametes with half the number of chromosomes.
During sexual reproduction, male and female gametes join to make a zygote, restoring the original number of chromosomes.
In flowering plants, meiosis produces spores with half the number of chromosomes; the gametes produced by the new generation join to make a zygote with a full set.
Crossing over creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes, and each chromosome in the gametes carries a unique set of genes.
When diverse gametes combine, the zygote is genetically different from both parents, so meiosis contributes to genetic diversity.

written.text: What does calcium work in human body?
modelAnswer: Calcium is needed for the formation and strength of bones and teeth.
It also helps in blood clotting and muscle contraction.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either blood clotting or muscle contraction.

written.text: What is Lacteal?
modelAnswer: A lacteal is a lymph vessel present in a villus of the small intestine.

written.text: What are causes of Leukaemia?
modelAnswer: Leukaemia involves abnormal, uncontrolled production of white blood cells; its exact cause is not always known.
Possible causes or risk factors include exposure to radiation and certain harmful chemicals.
Genetic changes and some viral infections may also be involved.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for genetic changes, mutation or a viral cause.

written.text: How would you distinguish between bicuspid and tricuspid valves?
modelAnswer: The bicuspid (mitral) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle and has two cusps.
The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle and has three cusps.

written.text: Explain shortly the organ system level.
modelAnswer: An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform a particular major function.

written.text: What is the function of arteries in human body? Write any two functions.
modelAnswer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body organs.

written.text: Write note on Molecular level of organization.
modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine to form molecules, which are the building materials of cell structures and organelles.
Molecules in organisms include organic molecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
Inorganic substances such as water, minerals and carbon dioxide are also present at this level.

written.text: Explain white blood cells.
modelAnswer: White blood cells, also called leucocytes, protect the body against pathogens and disease.
They can move out of blood vessels and engulf pathogens by phagocytosis.
Some white blood cells, such as lymphocytes, produce antibodies that help destroy pathogens.
White blood cells have a nucleus and do not contain haemoglobin.

written.text: What is population level? Give an example.
modelAnswer: Population level is a group of individuals of the same species living in a particular area at a particular time.

written.text: Describe the muscle tissue along with its types.
modelAnswer: Muscle tissue is made of cells that contract and produce movement.
Skeletal or striated muscle is usually attached to bones and is voluntary.
Smooth or non-striated muscle is found in the walls of internal organs and is involuntary.
Cardiac muscle is found in the heart and is involuntary.

rubric.description: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and is found in the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying cardiac muscle as involuntary and stating that it is found in the heart.

modelAnswer: Observe a prepared smooth-muscle slide under a microscope: the fibres are spindle-shaped, each with a single nucleus.

written.text: What role does the pericardial fluid play?
modelAnswer: Pericardial fluid lies between the membranes surrounding the heart.

written.text: Write a comprehensive note on cellular organizations by explaining various types of organisms.
modelAnswer: In unicellular organisms, a single cell performs all the functions needed for life; for example, Amoeba.
In colonial organisms, similar cells live together in a group or colony; Volvox is an example.
Multicellular organisms consist of many cells, often specialized for different functions; humans are an example.
Specialized cells work together through division of labour and may form tissues and organs.

written.text: What do you know about the stomach in human body? Write down its structure and functions.
modelAnswer: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped sac in the upper abdomen, between the oesophagus and small intestine.
Its inner lining contains gastric glands that secrete gastric juice, including hydrochloric acid, pepsin, and protective mucus.
The stomach temporarily stores food and churns it, mixing it with gastric juice.
Hydrochloric acid provides an acidic medium and helps kill microbes.
Pepsin begins protein digestion, and the partly digested food becomes semi-liquid chyme.

rubric.description: It lies between the oesophagus and the small intestine.

modelAnswer: The sound lubb is produced when the atrioventricular valves close as the ventricles begin to contract.

At the cell level, organelles are organized within a cell and perform specific functions.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

written.text: How small intestine helps the human body to digest food?
modelAnswer: In the small intestine, pancreatic juice supplies enzymes that digest carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
Bile from the liver neutralizes acidic food arriving from the stomach and emulsifies fats into small droplets.
Enzymes in the intestinal juice complete the digestion of food into simple, soluble molecules.
The inner surface has many villi, which provide a large surface area for absorption.
Glucose and amino acids pass into the blood, while many products of fat digestion enter the lacteals.

written.text: Describe the disorders of Gut in detail.
modelAnswer: Diarrhoea is the frequent passage of loose, watery stools. It causes excessive loss of water and salts and may lead to dehydration.

written.text: Describe digestion and Absorption of food in small intestine.

The inner lining has villi that absorb digested nutrients; glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries, while fatty acids and glycerol enter lacteals.
Blood and lymph carry the absorbed nutrients from the small intestine to the body cells.

written.text: Write the structure of Human Heart with Diagram.
modelAnswer: The heart is a hollow, muscular organ enclosed by a protective covering; it has four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle.

The venae cavae bring deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium; it passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and leaves through the pulmonary artery for the lungs.
Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium; it passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve to the left ventricle and leaves through the aorta for the body.

written.text: Human heart acts like a double pump. Explain it.
modelAnswer: The human heart acts as a double pump because its right and left sides pump blood through two separate circuits.
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary arteries; this is pulmonary circulation.
In the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and receives oxygen.
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body through the aorta; this is systemic circulation.
Blood returns from the body to the right side of the heart, and from the lungs to the left side.

written.text: Explain the levels of organization in multicellular organism. How does each level contribute to the overall functioning of an organism?
modelAnswer: Atoms are the smallest unit of matter that maintain the property of an element.
Atoms combine to form molecules.
Molecules combine in specific ways to make organelles, each specialized for a particular function.
Organelles assemble and interact to make cells, the smallest units with characteristics of life.
Similar cells work together in tissues to perform specific functions.
Related tissues work together in organs to perform specific functions.
Multiple organs work together in organ systems to perform related functions.

written.text: Explain the levels of organization in multicellular organism. How does each level contribute to the overall functioning of an organism?
modelAnswer: An organelle is a specialised structure within a cell, and organelles help the cell perform its functions.
Cells with similar functions group together to form tissues.
Different tissues work together to form an organ, which performs particular functions.
Organs that work together form an organ system.
Organ systems coordinate their activities so the whole organism can function and maintain life.

written.text: What is a tissue level? Explain plant and animal tissues.
modelAnswer: The tissue level is a level of organization in which groups of similar cells work together to perform a particular function.
Plant tissues include epidermal tissue, mesophyll, xylem, and phloem.
Epidermal tissue protects the plant, mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, xylem transports water, and phloem transports food.
Animal tissues include epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissues, each specialised for particular functions.

Palisade mesophyll contains many chloroplasts and carries out most photosynthesis.
Spongy mesophyll has air spaces that support gas exchange.
Xylem brings water to the leaf, and phloem transports food from it to other parts of the plant.

written.text: Define homeostasis and explain its importance. Discuss how different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.
modelAnswer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions in an organism.
It is important because cells and organs need suitable conditions to function properly.
Different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.
The digestive system supplies nutrients, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, and the circulatory system transports materials around the body.
The excretory system removes wastes, helping keep the internal conditions stable.

written.text: Evaluate the importance of organ systems working in harmony and predict the consequences of a failure in one system on the others.
modelAnswer: Organ systems work in harmony because each depends on the others to carry out the body's life functions.
Together, they supply and transport useful materials, remove wastes, and maintain homeostasis.
If one system fails, other systems may not receive the oxygen, nutrients, or materials they need.
Wastes may also build up if the system responsible for their removal is not working.
As a result, the function of other systems and the whole body may be disrupted.

written.text:

modelAnswer: (a) Blood disorders are diseases that affect blood cells, blood components or the ability of blood to clot.
Anemia is a reduction in red blood cells or haemoglobin, which decreases the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity.
Leukemia is cancer involving the abnormal production of white blood cells.
Hemophilia is an inherited disorder in which blood does not clot normally, so bleeding may continue for a long time.
Thalassemia is an inherited disorder that affects the production of haemoglobin.
(b) Population level: A population consists of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
Community level: A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.

modelAnswer: (a) When food molecules are oxidized in cells, their chemical energy is released.
One gram of lipid yields about 9 kcal, while one gram of protein yields about 4 kcal.
One gram of carbohydrate also yields about 4 kcal.
Therefore, lipids are the most concentrated energy source per gram; the statement is not fully correct if it calls proteins the best energy source as well.
Proteins can be used for energy, but their main roles are growth and repair, and they are not normally the body's preferred fuel.
(b) Sources of proteins include meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses, beans and nuts.
Proteins are needed for the growth and repair of body tissues.
They form enzymes, antibodies and some hormones.
They also form body structures such as muscles; proteins can be used as an energy source when needed.

written.text:
(a) Write a note on carbohydrates and proteins.
(b) Explain structure, function, importance and sources of lipids.
modelAnswer: (a) Carbohydrates are organic compounds made mainly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
They are an important source of energy; glucose and starch are examples.
Proteins are made of amino acids and contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen.
Proteins are needed for growth and repair of body tissues.
They also form enzymes and antibodies and are important components of muscles.
(b) Lipids are organic compounds containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; they contain less oxygen than carbohydrates.
Many lipids are formed from glycerol and fatty acids and are insoluble in water.
Lipids store energy, form part of cell membranes, and provide insulation and protection.
Sources include vegetable oils, butter, ghee, nuts, seeds, meat and milk.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all three components.

rubric.why: Checks that the structure shows adenosine linked to three phosphate groups.
rubric.description: A labeled structure showing adenine and ribose linked to three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a structure showing adenine, ribose and the chain of three phosphate groups.

written.text: Sketch molecular structure of ATP.
modelAnswer: Draw and label the parts in this order: adenine — ribose — phosphate — phosphate — phosphate.
Show adenine attached to ribose; label this combined part “adenosine.”
Attach three phosphate groups in a chain to the ribose, and label the molecule “ATP.”
written.followUp: Sketch and label the structure of an ATP molecule.

rubric.why: ATP contains adenine attached to a ribose sugar; together these form adenosine.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark if both adenine and ribose (or sugar) are shown and labelled.

rubric.why: Three phosphate groups are attached to the ribose part of ATP.
rubric.description: Shows three phosphate groups attached to adenosine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing and labelling three phosphate groups linked to the adenine–ribose part.

written.text: Define aerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the process in which glucose is completely broken down in the presence of oxygen.
It releases energy and produces carbon dioxide and water.
written.followUp: Define anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Identifies that aerobic respiration takes place when oxygen is present.
rubric.description: Aerobic respiration is respiration that takes place in the presence of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that oxygen is present or required.

rubric.why: Describes the complete breakdown of glucose and the products and energy released.
rubric.description: Glucose is completely broken down to carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy.
rubric.how: Award the mark for identifying complete glucose breakdown, carbon dioxide and water as products, and energy release.

written.text: Define photosynthesis. Also write its equation.
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
6CO2 + 6H2O --light and chlorophyll--> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
written.followUp: What raw materials and conditions are required for photosynthesis?

rubric.why: A definition should explain that plants produce food or glucose using light energy.
rubric.description: Defines photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining photosynthesis as food or glucose production by plants using light.

rubric.why: The equation must show the reactants, products, and balanced quantities.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced photosynthesis equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly balanced equation, in symbols or named substances.

written.text: What is lactic acid fermentation?
modelAnswer: Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose, occurring when oxygen is unavailable.
It produces lactic acid and releases a small amount of energy.
written.followUp: What is alcoholic fermentation, and what are its products?

rubric.why: Identifies the process as an anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.description: States that lactic acid fermentation takes place without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the process as anaerobic or stating that it occurs in the absence of oxygen.

rubric.why: Names the characteristic product of this type of fermentation.
rubric.description: Names lactic acid as the product of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming lactic acid as a product; energy release may also be mentioned.

written.text: What is alcoholic fermentation?
modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
It produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
written.followUp: What are the products of lactic acid fermentation?

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation is an anaerobic process involving the breakdown of glucose.
rubric.description: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen.

rubric.why: Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the characteristic products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: It produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both products.

written.text: Write the role of ATP for the cell.
modelAnswer: ATP acts as the cell's immediate energy source and transfers energy where it is needed.
It provides energy for cellular activities.
written.followUp: How does ATP provide energy for cellular activities?

rubric.why: ATP is the cell's immediate energy source or energy currency.
rubric.description: Identifies ATP as a source or carrier of energy for the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for ATP's energy role.

rubric.why: ATP supplies energy to drive cellular activities.
rubric.description: States that ATP powers cellular activities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining what the energy is used for.

written.text: Write a note on energy budget of respiration.
modelAnswer: For the textbook energy budget of aerobic respiration, one glucose molecule yields:
Glycolysis: 2 ATP.
Krebs cycle: 2 ATP.
Electron transport chain: 34 ATP.
Total: 2 + 2 + 34 = 38 ATP per glucose molecule.
written.followUp: State how many ATP are formed in glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain during aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule.

rubric.why: Glycolysis yields a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Gives the ATP yield from glycolysis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2 ATP from glycolysis.

rubric.why: The Krebs cycle yields 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Gives the ATP yield from the Krebs cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2 ATP from the Krebs cycle.

rubric.why: The electron transport chain yields 34 ATP in the textbook energy budget.
rubric.description: Gives the ATP yield from the electron transport chain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 34 ATP from the electron transport chain.

rubric.why: The textbook total is 38 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Gives the total ATP yield.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct total.

written.text: What is effect of light intensity and temperature in photosynthesis?
modelAnswer: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until it reaches a maximum or another factor becomes limiting.
As temperature rises, the rate increases up to an optimum; above it, the rate falls because photosynthetic enzymes denature.
written.followUp: Explain how carbon dioxide concentration affects the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Light provides energy for photosynthesis, so increasing its intensity raises the rate up to a limit.
rubric.description: States the effect of increasing light intensity on photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the rate increases with light intensity until another factor limits it or the rate reaches a maximum.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled: warming increases its rate up to an optimum, while excessive heat damages enzymes.
rubric.description: Describes the effect of temperature, including the optimum or decline at high temperature.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the rate rises to an optimum and then falls at high temperature due to enzyme denaturation.

written.text: Explain the limiting factors in photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: The rate of photosynthesis is limited by factors that are in short supply or at unsuitable levels.
As light intensity increases, the rate usually increases until another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration can increase the rate because carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum; excessive temperature can damage enzymes and reduce the rate.
written.followUp: Describe how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: A limiting factor restricts photosynthesis when it is in short supply or at an unsuitable level.
rubric.description: Explains what a limiting factor is.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that a limiting factor restricts the rate because it is in short supply or at an unsuitable level.

rubric.why: Increasing light intensity raises the rate until another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased light intensity to an increased rate, usually until another factor limits it.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis, and more of it can increase the rate.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing carbon dioxide availability can increase the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: The rate rises with temperature up to an optimum; excessive heat can damage enzymes and reduce the rate.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the optimum temperature effect and the effect of excessive heat on enzymes or the rate.

written.text: What is meant by light reactions?
modelAnswer: Light reactions are the photosynthetic reactions that require light.
They occur in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast, where chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
written.followUp: Where do light reactions occur in a chloroplast?

rubric.why: Dependence on light is the defining feature of light reactions.
rubric.description: States that these reactions require light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their dependence on light.

rubric.why: Light reactions occur on the chlorophyll-containing thylakoid membranes, arranged in grana.
rubric.description: Identifies the site of light reactions in the chloroplast.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming thylakoids or grana.

written.text: What is cellular respiration?
modelAnswer: Cellular respiration is the series of reactions in cells in which glucose is broken down.
This process releases energy for the cell.
written.followUp: State the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Cellular respiration involves the breakdown or oxidation of glucose in cells.
rubric.description: Defines cellular respiration as the breakdown or oxidation of glucose in cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying glucose as being broken down or oxidised.

rubric.why: Respiration releases energy that the cell can use.
rubric.description: States that cellular respiration releases energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the release of energy.

written.text: Describe alcoholic fermentation.
modelAnswer: In the absence of oxygen, yeast breaks down glucose by alcoholic fermentation.
Glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 carbon dioxide + energy.
written.followUp: What is lactic acid fermentation, and in which cells does it occur?

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation is an anaerobic process commonly carried out by yeast.
rubric.description: States that yeast breaks down glucose in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying yeast and the absence of oxygen.

rubric.why: Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products that identify alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: Identifies ethanol and carbon dioxide as the products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both products or giving their chemical formulae.

written.text: Differentiate between Alcoholic Fermentation and Lactic Acid Fermentation.
modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation: In the absence of oxygen, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Lactic acid fermentation: In the absence of oxygen, glucose is converted into lactic acid, as in muscle cells.
written.followUp: Differentiate between alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: States that alcoholic fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking ethanol and carbon dioxide with alcoholic fermentation.

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic product of lactic acid fermentation.
rubric.description: States that lactic acid fermentation produces lactic acid, for example in muscle cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying lactic acid as the product.

written.text: Define Oxidation and Reduction.
modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, addition of oxygen, or removal of hydrogen.
Reduction is the gain of electrons, removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen.
written.followUp: Explain oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.

rubric.why: Gives a valid definition of oxidation.
rubric.description: Defines oxidation as loss of electrons, addition of oxygen, or removal of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct definition of oxidation.

rubric.why: Gives a valid definition of reduction.
rubric.description: Defines reduction as gain of electrons, removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct definition of reduction.

written.text: What is meant by photolysis of water?
modelAnswer: Photolysis of water is the splitting of water molecules by light energy during photosynthesis.
It produces oxygen, hydrogen ions (protons) and electrons; oxygen is released, while the hydrogen ions and electrons are used in photosynthesis.
written.followUp: What products are formed when water undergoes photolysis during photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Checks that photolysis means the splitting of water using light energy.
rubric.description: Splitting of water by light
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that light energy splits water molecules.

rubric.why: Checks for the products of water splitting.
rubric.description: Products of photolysis
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying oxygen and hydrogen (including hydrogen ions and electrons) as products.

written.text: Define cellular respiration. Give its importance.
modelAnswer: Cellular respiration is the breakdown or oxidation of food, especially glucose, in cells to release energy.
This energy is used to carry out life activities and metabolic processes.
written.followUp: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration and state one activity that requires its energy.

rubric.why: Cellular respiration is the breakdown or oxidation of food in cells, releasing energy.
rubric.description: Definition of cellular respiration
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining respiration as the cellular breakdown or oxidation of food that releases energy.

rubric.why: The released energy powers the activities of the organism, including metabolic processes.
rubric.description: Importance of cellular respiration
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that respiration supplies energy for life or metabolic activities.

written.text: How alcohol is formed. Write its equation.
modelAnswer: In the absence of oxygen, yeast ferments glucose to form ethanol (ethyl alcohol) and carbon dioxide.
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy
written.followUp: Write the equation for aerobic respiration and name the gas required for it.

rubric.why: Yeast forms ethanol (ethyl alcohol) by fermenting glucose in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.description: How alcohol is formed
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing yeast fermentation of glucose under anaerobic conditions to form alcohol.

rubric.why: The fermentation equation shows glucose producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.description: Equation for alcohol formation
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation or equivalent word equation.

written.text: Describe the term “Anaerobes” with two Suitable examples.
modelAnswer: Anaerobes are organisms that can live or grow without oxygen.
Examples include yeast and Clostridium bacteria.
written.followUp: Define facultative anaerobes and give two examples.

rubric.why: Gives the defining feature of anaerobes.
rubric.description: Anaerobes are organisms that can live or grow without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they live or grow in the absence of oxygen.

rubric.why: The question requires two suitable examples.
rubric.description: Examples include yeast and anaerobic bacteria such as Clostridium.
rubric.how: Award for two suitable examples; accept other valid anaerobic organisms.

written.text: What is meant by Photosystems and also give their Location?
modelAnswer: Photosystems are groups of pigment molecules and proteins that absorb light energy.
They are located in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
written.followUp: What is the function of photosystems in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Explains what photosystems are or what they do.
rubric.description: Photosystems are groups of pigment molecules and proteins that absorb light energy.
rubric.how: Award for identifying photosystems as pigment-protein groups or stating that they absorb light.

rubric.why: Identifies the location of photosystems.
rubric.description: Photosystems are located in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award for locating photosystems in the thylakoid membrane(s) of chloroplasts.

written.text: Write full form of FADH₂ and NADH.
modelAnswer: FADH₂ stands for flavin adenine dinucleotide (in its reduced form).
NADH stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (in its reduced form).
written.followUp: Write the full forms of ATP and ADP.

rubric.why: Checks the correct expansion of FADH₂.
rubric.description: Expands FAD as flavin adenine dinucleotide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct full form.

rubric.why: Checks the correct expansion of NADH.
rubric.description: Expands NAD as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct full form.

written.text: What are the Limiting Factors of Photosynthesis?
modelAnswer: The main limiting factors of photosynthesis include light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.
Water availability and the amount of chlorophyll can also limit the rate of photosynthesis.
written.followUp: Name three factors that can affect the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies a major factor affecting photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Names light intensity as a limiting factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming light or light intensity.

rubric.why: Identifies another accepted limiting factor.
rubric.description: Names at least one other limiting factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration, temperature, water, or chlorophyll.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any one additional valid factor.

written.text: Why it is incorrect to say that the energy releasing step of respiration is ETC (Electron transport chain)
modelAnswer: It is incorrect to call the ETC the only energy-releasing step because energy is also released during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.
The ETC is the final stage; energy released as electrons pass along carriers is used to form ATP.
written.followUp: What is the role of the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration?

rubric.why: Energy is released during other stages of respiration as well as during the ETC.
rubric.description: Explains that energy release is not limited to the ETC.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming glycolysis or the Krebs cycle as another stage where energy is released.

rubric.why: The ETC is the final stage in which electron transfer releases energy used to form ATP.
rubric.description: Describes the ETC as an electron-transfer stage that helps form ATP, rather than the only energy-releasing step.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking electron transfer in the ETC with ATP formation.

written.text: How will you compare respiration with photosynthesis ?
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, storing light energy in glucose.
Respiration breaks down glucose, usually using oxygen, and releases energy while producing carbon dioxide and water.
written.followUp: State one way in which photosynthesis and respiration are opposite processes.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
rubric.description: States the reactants and products of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct photosynthesis comparison, including its use of carbon dioxide and water or production of glucose and oxygen.

rubric.why: Respiration breaks down glucose, generally using oxygen, and releases energy while producing carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.description: Compares respiration with photosynthesis as the reverse process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that respiration breaks down glucose and releases energy, or for correctly giving its products in contrast to photosynthesis.

written.text: What is the energy budget of respiration ? Explain it
modelAnswer: The energy budget of respiration is the accounting of ATP produced when one glucose molecule is completely oxidized.
Glycolysis produces a net 2 ATP.
The Krebs cycle produces 2 ATP.
The electron transport chain produces 34 ATP in the conventional textbook accounting.
Total ATP produced = 2 + 2 + 34 = 38 ATP per glucose molecule.
written.followUp: Explain how ATP is produced during aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule.

rubric.why: The energy budget describes ATP formed as glucose is broken down during respiration.
rubric.description: Introduce the energy budget of respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking glucose oxidation during respiration with ATP production.

rubric.why: Glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Give ATP yield from glycolysis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the net yield of 2 ATP from glycolysis.

rubric.why: The Krebs cycle yields 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Give ATP yield from the Krebs cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the 2 ATP formed in the Krebs cycle.

rubric.why: In the conventional textbook accounting, most ATP is produced in the electron transport chain.
rubric.description: Give ATP yield from the electron transport chain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the conventional yield of 34 ATP from the electron transport chain.

rubric.why: The conventional total energy budget is 38 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: State the total ATP yield.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a total of 38 ATP per glucose molecule using the textbook accounting.

written.text: Differentiate between light and dark reaction of photosynthesis
modelAnswer: The light reaction occurs in the thylakoids (grana), requires light, and produces ATP, NADPH and oxygen.
The dark reaction occurs in the stroma; it uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and does not directly require light.
written.followUp: Compare the light-dependent and light-independent stages of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Award for a correct feature of the light reaction.
rubric.description: The light reaction takes place in the thylakoids (grana) and requires light.
rubric.how: Look for the light requirement and/or its location in the thylakoids or grana.

rubric.why: Award for a correct contrast describing the dark reaction.
rubric.description: The dark reaction occurs in the stroma and uses carbon dioxide and products of the light reaction to make carbohydrates.
rubric.how: Look for its location in the stroma and/or the use of carbon dioxide with ATP and NADPH to form carbohydrates; accept that it does not directly require light.

written.text: Do you think that the food is oxidized without oxygen ? How and by which methods ?
modelAnswer: Yes. Food can be broken down in the absence of oxygen by anaerobic respiration, an incomplete breakdown of glucose.
In yeast, anaerobic respiration is called fermentation and produces ethanol, carbon dioxide and a small amount of energy.
In muscle cells, glucose may be broken down without oxygen to form lactic acid and release a small amount of energy.
written.followUp: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration, giving the products of each.

rubric.why: Answers that food can be broken down without oxygen and names the process.
rubric.description: Yes. Food can be broken down in the absence of oxygen by anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear yes and identification of anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Identifies the conditions or nature of the process.
rubric.description: Anaerobic respiration is an incomplete breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the absence of oxygen or incomplete breakdown.

rubric.why: Names a common organism or method associated with anaerobic breakdown.
rubric.description: In yeast, this process is called fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying yeast or fermentation.

rubric.why: Gives the products of anaerobic breakdown in yeast or muscle cells.
rubric.description: Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscle cells can produce lactic acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct product set.

rubric.why: Notes that anaerobic respiration releases energy.
rubric.description: The process releases a small amount of energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that energy is released.

written.text: Why oxidation reduction reaction is called redox reaction?
modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, while reduction is the gain of electrons.
In a reaction, oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously; therefore, it is called a redox reaction.
written.followUp: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.

rubric.why: Tests the electron-transfer definition of oxidation.
rubric.description: States that oxidation is the loss of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining oxidation as loss of electrons.

rubric.why: Tests the paired nature of oxidation and reduction in a redox reaction.
rubric.description: Explains that reduction is gain of electrons and that oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the two processes occur together; accept the electron-transfer definition of reduction when it is correctly paired with oxidation.

written.text: What do you know about the accessory pigments?
modelAnswer: Accessory pigments include chlorophyll b and carotenoids, such as carotenes and xanthophylls.
They absorb light wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a for photosynthesis.
written.followUp: Name two accessory pigments and state how they help in photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Award for identifying accessory pigments.
rubric.description: Names accessory pigments such as chlorophyll b and carotenoids.
rubric.how: Accept either a correct pigment name or group of pigments.

rubric.why: Accessory pigments broaden the range of light absorbed for photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Explains that accessory pigments absorb light and transfer its energy to chlorophyll a.
rubric.how: Require the idea of light absorption and energy transfer to chlorophyll a.

written.text: How alcoholic fermentation differs from lactic acid fermentation?
modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation, commonly carried out by yeast, produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Lactic acid fermentation, which occurs in some bacteria and in muscle cells, produces lactic acid.
written.followUp: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration in yeast.

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, commonly in yeast.
rubric.description: States the products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ethanol and carbon dioxide as its products.

rubric.why: Lactic acid fermentation produces lactic acid rather than ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.description: States the product of lactic acid fermentation and distinguishes it from alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying lactic acid as the product; accept mention of muscle cells or bacteria as the site.

written.text: Write the role of light intensity on the process of photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases while light is a limiting factor.
At high light intensity, the rate levels off because another factor becomes limiting.
written.followUp: How does carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Increasing light intensity generally increases the rate of photosynthesis when light is limiting.
rubric.description: States the effect of increasing light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking greater light intensity with a higher photosynthesis rate, or low light with a low rate.

rubric.why: The rate eventually levels off when another factor becomes limiting or the light response reaches saturation.
rubric.description: Describes the limit to the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate stops increasing at high intensity because another factor becomes limiting or the rate reaches saturation.

written.text: Write differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen.

Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose to carbon dioxide and water, whereas anaerobic respiration incompletely breaks it down, producing lactic acid in muscles or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast.
Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.
Aerobic respiration mainly occurs in the mitochondria, while anaerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm.
written.followUp: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in terms of oxygen use, products and energy released.

rubric.why: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen, whereas anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen.
rubric.description: Compares oxygen requirements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the oxygen requirement of the two processes.

rubric.why: Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose, while anaerobic products include lactic acid or ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.description: Compares the products or completeness of breakdown.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly giving the products or stating that aerobic breakdown is complete and anaerobic breakdown is incomplete.

rubric.why: Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.
rubric.description: Compares energy released.

rubric.why: The processes differ in cellular location, and both break down glucose to release energy.

written.text: What is meant by photosystem?
modelAnswer: A photosystem is a group of pigment molecules, including chlorophyll, arranged in the thylakoid membrane.

written.text: Define fermentation and write the names of its two types.
modelAnswer: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to release energy.
Its two types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
written.followUp: Name the products of alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

rubric.why: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose, releasing energy.
rubric.description: Defines fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing fermentation as the breakdown of glucose without oxygen, with energy release.

rubric.why: The two types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in green plants absorbs light energy.

written.text: Who discovered ATP and who named it as an energy transfer molecule in the living cell?
modelAnswer: ATP was discovered by Karl Lohmann in 1929.

written.text: Differentiate between oxidation and reduction reaction.
modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, addition of oxygen, or removal of hydrogen.
Reduction is the gain of electrons, removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen.

written.text: State how the light intensity, concentration of carbondioxide and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis?
modelAnswer: Increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis because light supplies the energy for the process; the rate levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate because carbon dioxide is a raw material; the rate also levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum because photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes.
Above the optimum temperature, the rate decreases as the enzymes lose their proper functioning.
written.followUp: Explain how increasing light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affects photosynthesis, including the effect of a limiting factor.

rubric.why: Light supplies energy for photosynthesis, and greater intensity raises the rate up to a limit.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so increasing its concentration raises the rate up to a limit.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate.

written.text: Explain the mechanism of respiration while defining the glycolysis, krebs cycle and electron transport chain.
modelAnswer: Cellular respiration is the process in which cells break down glucose and release energy, which is transferred to ATP.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvic acid, producing a small amount of ATP and NADH.
In the mitochondrial matrix, the Krebs cycle oxidizes products of pyruvic acid breakdown, releasing carbon dioxide and producing energy carriers.
In the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, electrons pass along carriers; oxygen accepts electrons and forms water, and much ATP is produced.

written.text: Write detail of light reactions of photosynthesis and also draw diagram.
modelAnswer: The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast, where chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
Light energy drives photolysis: water is split into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; oxygen is released.
Light-excited electrons pass through electron carriers, and their energy is used to form ATP.
Electrons reaching photosystem I help reduce NADP to NADPH (reduced NADP).
The ATP and NADPH formed are used in the subsequent reactions of photosynthesis.
Diagram (schematic): H₂O → O₂ + H⁺ + e⁻; light → Photosystem II → electron transport chain → Photosystem I → NADP⁺ → NADPH.
Label ATP formation from the electron transport chain, and show light entering both photosystems.

modelAnswer: The light-dependent reaction is the stage of photosynthesis in which chlorophyll absorbs light energy and converts it into chemical energy in ATP and NADPH.
Water is split, releasing oxygen.

written.text: Define photosynthesis and write the equation of photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy, in the presence of chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
6CO₂ + 6H₂O —(light, chlorophyll)→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

written.text: How would you distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration? Explain anaerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen, whereas anaerobic respiration takes place without oxygen.
Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose; anaerobic respiration breaks it down incompletely.
Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water and releases more energy; anaerobic respiration releases less energy.
Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete breakdown of glucose without oxygen in the cytoplasm.
In yeast it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; in muscle cells it produces lactic acid.

written.text: Describe the role of electron transport chain during cellular respiration.

The energy released helps build a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis; oxygen combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

written.text: Define bioenergetics and explain that why ATP is called as cell's Energy Currency.
modelAnswer: Bioenergetics is the study of energy relationships and energy transformations in living organisms.
ATP (adenosine triphosphate) stores energy in its high-energy phosphate bonds.
When ATP is hydrolysed, it breaks down into ADP and phosphate and releases usable energy.
This energy is transferred to cellular processes that require energy.
ATP is therefore called the cell's energy currency.

written.text: Write the summary events of light reactions of Photosynthesis.

Electrons pass along an electron transport chain, and their energy is used to form ATP by photophosphorylation.
NADP accepts electrons and hydrogen ions and is reduced to NADPH.
Oxygen is released as a by-product; ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reactions.

written.text: What are limiting factors in photosynthesis? Explain.
modelAnswer: A limiting factor is a condition in short supply that restricts the rate of photosynthesis.
Light intensity affects the rate: as light intensity increases, the rate rises until another factor becomes limiting.
Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis; a low concentration limits the rate, while increasing it raises the rate up to a limit.
Temperature affects the enzymes involved in photosynthesis; low temperatures slow the reactions and very high temperatures can damage enzymes.
Water and chlorophyll are also necessary, and a shortage of either can limit photosynthesis.

written.text: Write a detailed note on electron transport chain.
modelAnswer: The electron transport chain is present in the inner mitochondrial membrane and consists of a series of electron carriers, including cytochromes.
NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the chain; as electrons pass from carrier to carrier, energy is released.
This energy pumps hydrogen ions across the inner membrane, creating a proton gradient.

Hydrogen ions flow back through ATP synthase, which uses the energy to make ATP from ADP and phosphate; oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

written.text: What is meant by aerobic respiration? Explain its three main stages.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm: one glucose molecule is split into two pyruvic acid molecules, with a small amount of ATP produced.
The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondria: products derived from pyruvate are oxidized, carbon dioxide is released, and energy is transferred to electron carriers.
The electron transport chain occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane: electrons pass along carriers, oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water, and most ATP is produced.

written.text: What is Anaerobic Respiration? Give its types in detail.

In lactic acid fermentation, as in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient, glucose produces lactic acid and a small amount of energy: glucose → 2 lactic acid + energy.
Lactic acid fermentation also occurs in some bacteria, such as Lactobacillus.

written.text: Describe mechanism of respiration.
modelAnswer: During inhalation, the external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs upwards and outwards.

The diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped, decreasing the volume of the chest cavity and raising its pressure; air is pushed out of the lungs.

written.text: What are Dark Reactions of Photosynthesis Mechanism? Write its events.
modelAnswer: Dark reactions, or the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of chloroplasts and do not require light directly.

PGA is reduced to PGAL using ATP and NADPH produced during the light reactions.
Some PGAL is used to make glucose and other carbohydrates.
The remaining PGAL is used to regenerate RuBP, allowing the cycle to continue.

written.text: Describe summary of the events of light reactions with diagram.
modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in photosystems absorbs light energy.

Light excites electrons again in photosystem I; the electrons and hydrogen are used to reduce NADP to NADPH.
ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reactions; oxygen is released.

written.text: Describe events in dark reactions in detail.
modelAnswer: The dark reactions, also called the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of the chloroplast and do not directly require light.

The unstable compound immediately splits into molecules of phosphoglycerate (PGA), a three-carbon compound.
Using ATP and NADPH produced in the light reactions, PGA is reduced to phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).
Some PGAL is used to form glucose and other carbohydrates; the remaining PGAL is used, with energy from ATP, to regenerate RuBP.

Dark reactions (the Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma. They do not require light directly and use ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide.

ATP and NADPH reduce PGA to PGAL (G3P).

written.text: Write Mechanism of Respiration.
modelAnswer: The overall equation is: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP).
During glycolysis, glucose is broken down into pyruvic acid in the cytoplasm.
When oxygen is available, pyruvic acid is further broken down in the mitochondria.
This complete breakdown produces carbon dioxide and water.
Energy is released and captured in ATP.

written.text: Describe different steps of light reactions. Also draw Z-scheme.
modelAnswer: Light is absorbed by photosystem II (P680), exciting electrons; photolysis of water replaces these electrons and releases oxygen and protons.
Electrons pass along an electron transport chain from PSII towards photosystem I; the released energy helps form ATP.
Light excites electrons in photosystem I (P700); they pass to ferredoxin and help reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.
Z-scheme (energy rises upward): H₂O → PSII (P680) ↗ primary acceptor → electron transport chain (ATP formed) → PSI (P700) ↗ primary acceptor → ferredoxin → NADP⁺ reductase → NADPH.

written.text: Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.
modelAnswer: ATP is a nucleotide made of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
The covalent bonds between two phosphates are high-energy bonds.
When the outer phosphate bond breaks, Pi separates and energy is released; ATP becomes ADP.
The breaking of one phosphate bond releases about 7.3 kcal per mole of ATP.
Cells use energy from food to combine ADP with Pi to form ATP.
ATP is made during energy-releasing processes and broken down during energy-consuming processes, so it transfers energy between metabolic reactions.

written.text: Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm: one glucose molecule is broken into two pyruvic acid molecules, with two ATP and two NADH formed.
When oxygen is available, pyruvic acid moves to the mitochondrial matrix and is converted into acetyl coenzyme-A.
In the Krebs cycle, acetyl coenzyme-A is completely oxidized to carbon dioxide, forming ATP, NADH and FADH₂.
The electron transport chain occurs on the inner membranes of mitochondria; electron flow releases energy used to make ATP.
At the end of the chain, electrons and hydrogen ions combine with oxygen to form water.

written.text: Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and NADH.
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is further broken down; the Krebs cycle releases carbon dioxide and transfers energy to carriers.
Electrons pass along the electron transport chain in the mitochondrion.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with hydrogen to form water.
Most ATP is produced during the electron transport chain.

written.text:
(a) Differentiate between aerobic and anaerobic respiration
(b) Write a note on energy budget of respiration.
modelAnswer: (a) Aerobic respiration occurs in the presence of oxygen; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen.
In aerobic respiration, glucose is completely broken down into carbon dioxide and water.
In anaerobic respiration, glucose is incompletely broken down into lactic acid in muscles, or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast.
Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration. (Textbooks may give about 36–38 ATP compared with 2 ATP.)
Aerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm and mitochondria; anaerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm.
(b) For the textbook energy budget of aerobic respiration, one glucose molecule yields:
Glycolysis: 2 ATP.
Krebs cycle: 2 ATP.
Electron transport chain: 34 ATP.
Total: 2 + 2 + 34 = 38 ATP per glucose molecule.

written.text:
(a) Explain mechanism of respiration.
(b) Explain the limiting factors in photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: (a) Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP).
First, glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvic acid.
In the mitochondria, pyruvic acid is further broken down in the Krebs cycle, releasing carbon dioxide.
Electrons pass along the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane; oxygen is the final electron acceptor and water is formed.
Energy released in these stages is captured mainly in ATP.
(b) The rate of photosynthesis is limited by factors that are in short supply or at unsuitable levels.
As light intensity increases, the rate usually increases until another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration can increase the rate because carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum; excessive temperature can damage enzymes and reduce the rate.

written.text:
(a) Describe the mechanism of respiration.
(b) Write differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: (a) During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, while the external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs up and out.
The volume of the chest cavity increases and its pressure decreases, so air enters the lungs.
During exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped, while the ribs move down and in as the intercostal muscles relax.
The volume of the chest cavity decreases and its pressure increases, forcing air out of the lungs.
(b) Aerobic respiration requires oxygen; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen.

Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose to carbon dioxide and water, whereas anaerobic respiration incompletely breaks it down, producing lactic acid in muscles or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast.
Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.
Aerobic respiration mainly occurs in the mitochondria, while anaerobic respiration takes place in the cytoplasm.

written.text: How would you relate the internal structure of root with the uptake of water and salts?
modelAnswer: Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; their thin walls and large surface area provide an effective surface for absorbing water and mineral salts.
Water enters the root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis because the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root hairs, often by active transport against their concentration gradient using energy.
Water and ions then move through the cortex and endodermis towards the vascular tissue of the root.
They enter the xylem, which transports water and mineral salts upwards through the plant.

written.text: Define transpiration. Also describe the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
Increased light and temperature generally increase the rate of transpiration.
High humidity decreases transpiration, whereas dry air increases it.
Wind or moving air generally increases transpiration by carrying away moist air around the leaf.
A shortage of soil water may cause stomata to close, reducing transpiration.

written.text: Define turgor pressure.

written.text: What is the role of magnesium in plants?

Wind removes moist air around the leaf and increases transpiration.

Sugars are unloaded at the sinks; loading and unloading may involve active transport and energy.

written.text: Mention the different events causing the opening and closing of stomata.
modelAnswer: In light, potassium ions enter the guard cells, lowering their water potential.
Water enters the guard cells by osmosis, making them turgid; the stomatal pore opens.
In darkness, potassium ions leave the guard cells, raising their water potential.
Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis, making them flaccid; the stomatal pore closes.

written.text: How is the solute concentration helpful in opening and closing of stomata?
modelAnswer: When solute concentration in guard cells increases, water enters them by osmosis.
The guard cells become turgid and the stomata open.
When solutes and water leave, the guard cells become flaccid and the stomata close.
written.followUp: Explain how water movement in guard cells causes stomata to open and close.

rubric.why: An increase in guard-cell solutes draws water into the cells by osmosis, making them turgid and opening the stomata.
rubric.description: Explains how increased solute concentration leads to water uptake and opening of the stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the opening sequence: solutes increase, water enters, or guard cells become turgid and stomata open.

rubric.why: When guard cells lose solutes and water, they become flaccid and the stomata close.
rubric.description: Explains how solute and water loss leads to closure of the stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the closing sequence: solutes or water leave, guard cells become flaccid, or stomata close.

written.text: How do plants get water and ions from soil?
modelAnswer: Root hairs provide a large surface area in contact with the soil.
Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root cells by active transport, which requires energy.
Water and ions pass through the root tissues to the xylem for transport through the plant.

rubric.description: Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming osmosis as the process of water uptake.

rubric.why: States the process used to take up mineral ions.

written.text: Define minerals and write down the names of any two major minerals.

written.text: Why do you think that transpiration is a necessary evil for plants?
modelAnswer: Transpiration is an evil because excessive loss of water may cause a plant to wilt.
It is necessary because it creates a transpiration pull that helps transport water and minerals from roots to leaves.
It also helps cool the plant.

written.text: Write down a note on the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Light generally opens stomata and increases transpiration; darkness tends to reduce it.
Higher temperature increases evaporation and therefore increases transpiration.
High humidity reduces transpiration, while dry air increases it.
Wind increases transpiration by carrying away moist air around the leaf; a larger leaf area or more stomata also increases water loss, while a thick cuticle reduces it.
The availability of water in the soil also affects the rate: water shortage reduces transpiration.

written.text: Explain (with the help of diagram) what would happen when plant and animal cells are placed in a hypertonic solution?
modelAnswer: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves both plant and animal cells by osmosis.
The animal cell shrinks (crenates) because it has no cell wall to resist the loss of water.
In the plant cell, the protoplast loses water and contracts away from the cell wall; this is called plasmolysis.
The rigid cell wall remains in place and helps retain the plant cell's outer shape.
Diagram construction: draw an animal-cell circle 2 cm in diameter and a smaller, crenated outline inside it; label it “animal cell in hypertonic solution.”
Draw a plant-cell rectangle 4 cm long × 2.5 cm high; draw a smaller protoplast, about 2.5 cm × 1.2 cm, separated from the wall; label “cell wall,” “plasmolysed protoplast,” and “hypertonic solution.”
Draw at least two arrows pointing out of each cell and label them “water.”

written.text: What is turgor pressure?
modelAnswer: Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall.
It develops when water enters the cell by osmosis and the contents press against the wall.

written.text: Which structures are involved in transpiration in plants?
modelAnswer: Transpiration mainly occurs through the stomata.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the leaves.

Wind generally increases transpiration by removing moist air around the leaves.

modelAnswer: Compound tissues are made of different kinds of cells that work together to perform a common function.
Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma; it transports water and mineral salts through the plant.
Phloem consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma; it transports food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.

modelAnswer: A source is a plant part, such as a mature leaf, that produces and exports sugars; a sink is a part that uses or stores sugars, such as a growing region or tuber.

written.text: Explain different factors affecting the rate of transpiration.

written.text: Explain the Pressure-Flow Mechanism for the transport of food in plants.
modelAnswer: Leaves are sources because they produce sugars, mainly sucrose, by photosynthesis.
Sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes of the phloem at the source.
The increased solute concentration draws water from the xylem into the phloem by osmosis, raising the pressure in the sieve tubes.
At sinks, such as roots, fruits or storage organs, sugars are unloaded and used or stored; pressure is lower there.
This pressure difference drives the bulk flow of phloem sap from source to sink; water can return to the xylem.

written.text: Describe Pressureflow theory in detail.
modelAnswer: At a source, such as a leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem sieve tubes.
The increased sugar concentration lowers the water potential in the phloem, so water enters from the xylem by osmosis.
This raises the hydrostatic pressure in the phloem at the source.
The pressure difference drives phloem sap in bulk from the source towards a sink, such as a root or growing region.
At the sink, sugar is unloaded for use or storage; water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, reducing pressure there.

written.text: Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.

written.text: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
modelAnswer: Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant.
Transpiration of water from leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull.
A continuous water column in xylem extends from leaves to stem and to roots.
Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels and adhesion to xylem walls help create this continuous column.
When water moves up through the leaf xylem, it produces tension on the whole column, so the column is pulled upwards from roots towards leaves.
Dissolved salts are carried upwards with the water.

written.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, sucrose enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport.
Companion cells provide energy for this active transport.
The higher solute concentration in sieve tubes causes water to enter from nearby xylem by osmosis.
Fluid pressure in sieve tubes increases at the source, and the food solution flows towards the sink.
At the sink, sucrose is actively unloaded from sieve tubes into the sink tissues.
Water moves by osmosis from sieve tubes into the xylem, reducing fluid pressure in sieve tubes.
Because fluid pressure is higher at the source than at the sink, food flows in bulk towards the sink.

written.text: Describe temperature, wind and humidity as the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Higher temperature generally increases transpiration because evaporation and diffusion of water vapour become faster.
Wind usually increases transpiration by carrying away moist air from around the leaves.
High humidity decreases transpiration because the air already contains much water vapour.
This reduces the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air.
Final answer: Higher temperature and wind usually increase transpiration, while high humidity decreases it.

written.text: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism
modelAnswer: At the source, such as a leaf, sucrose is loaded into the phloem.
This lowers the water potential in the phloem, so water enters from nearby xylem by osmosis.
The entry of water raises the pressure in the phloem at the source.
Phloem sap moves down the pressure gradient towards a sink, where sucrose is unloaded for use or storage.
Water then moves out of the phloem, helping maintain the pressure difference between source and sink.
Final answer: Food moves in phloem from source to sink because water entry at the source creates a pressure gradient.

written.text: Explain osmotic adjustments in in hydrophytes, xerophytes and halophytes.
modelAnswer: Hydrophytes grow where water is abundant, so they generally need little osmotic adjustment to obtain water.
Xerophytes face water shortage; they can accumulate solutes in cells, lowering water potential and helping cells absorb or retain water.
Halophytes live in salty habitats, where the surrounding solution makes water uptake difficult.
They accumulate compatible solutes in their cytoplasm or store salts in vacuoles, helping maintain water uptake while limiting salt damage.
Final answer: Xerophytes and halophytes adjust cell solute concentrations to maintain water uptake; hydrophytes live where water is readily available.

written.text:
(a) How would you relate the internal structure of root with the uptake of water and salts?
(b) What are the environmental hazards related to the use of fertilizers?
modelAnswer: (a) Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; their thin walls and large surface area provide an effective surface for absorbing water and mineral salts.
Water enters the root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis because the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root hairs, often by active transport against their concentration gradient using energy.
Water and ions then move through the cortex and endodermis towards the vascular tissue of the root.
They enter the xylem, which transports water and mineral salts upwards through the plant.
(b) Rain may wash excess fertilizers from fields into rivers and lakes.
The added nutrients can cause eutrophication and excessive algal growth.
When the algae die, their decomposition uses dissolved oxygen; oxygen depletion can kill fish and other aquatic life.
Nitrates may also leach into groundwater, while excessive fertilizer use can damage soil through acidification or salinity.

written.text:

modelAnswer: (a) Root hairs absorb water from the soil, mainly by osmosis.
Water passes across the root cortex and enters the xylem.
Xylem vessels carry water and dissolved mineral salts upward through the stem to the leaves.
Transpiration from leaves creates a pull that draws the water column upward.
Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls help keep the column continuous; root pressure may also assist.
(b) Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
Increased light and temperature generally increase the rate of transpiration.
High humidity decreases transpiration, whereas dry air increases it.
Wind or moving air generally increases transpiration by carrying away moist air around the leaf.
A shortage of soil water may cause stomata to close, reducing transpiration.

written.text:

modelAnswer: (a) Compound tissues consist of different types of cells that work together to perform a common function.
Xylem is made up of vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots towards the leaves and also provides support.
Phloem is made up of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
Phloem transports (translocates) food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.
(b) Higher temperature increases evaporation of water from leaf surfaces and generally increases transpiration.
High humidity reduces the water-vapour gradient from the leaf to the air, so transpiration decreases; low humidity has the opposite effect.
Wind removes moist air around the leaf and increases transpiration.
Light usually causes stomata to open and increases transpiration; in darkness, stomata tend to close and the rate decreases.

written.text: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
modelAnswer: The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Microspores develop into pollen grains, which are the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The gametophytes produce gametes, and pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.
The pollen tube grows to the ovule and carries two sperms into the embryo sac.
One sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus that develops into endosperm.
The zygote develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.
A seed that gets suitable conditions can grow into the next sporophyte generation.

written.text: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
modelAnswer: The adult flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte (2n), which produces flowers.
Meiosis forms haploid spores. Microspores develop into pollen grains, the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The male gametophyte forms male gametes, and the female gametophyte contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.
After pollination, a pollen tube grows to the embryo sac and carries the male gametes.
One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. This is double fertilization.
The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed, which germinates to form a new sporophyte.

On the other hand, the reproduction that involves the fusion of male and female gametes is called sexual reproduction. In sexual reproduction, the offspring have variations among themselves and with the parents.

written.text:
(a) Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
(b) Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
modelAnswer: (a) The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.
The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Microspores develop into pollen grains, which are the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The gametophytes produce gametes, and pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.
The pollen tube grows to the ovule and carries two sperms into the embryo sac.
One sperm fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus that develops into endosperm.
The zygote develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.
A seed that gets suitable conditions can grow into the next sporophyte generation.
(b) During binary fission, the bacterial DNA replicates.
The daughter DNA molecules move to opposite sides.
The cell membrane pinches in.
A new cell wall is synthesized in the middle.
Two identical daughter bacteria are produced.
